Statement II: At constant temperature and pressure, a chemical or physical process is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy of the system is negative (\(\Delta G < 0\)).

Statement III: The standard Gibbs energy change of a reaction is related to its thermodynamic equilibrium constant by the equation \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: एक स्वतःप्रवर्तित प्रक्रम से गुजरने वाले विलगित निकाय के लिए आंतरिक ऊर्जा में परिवर्तन शून्य होता है (\(\Delta U = 0\)) जबकि एन्ट्रॉपी में कुल परिवर्तन धनात्मक होता है (\(\Delta S > 0\))।

कथन II: स्थिर ताप और दाब पर, कोई रासायनिक या भौतिक प्रक्रम स्वतःप्रवर्तित होता है यदि निकाय के गिब्ज़ ऊर्जा में परिवर्तन ऋणात्मक हो (\(\Delta G < 0\))।

कथन III: किसी अभिक्रिया का मानक गिब्ज़ ऊर्जा परिवर्तन उसके ऊष्मागतिक साम्य स्थिरांक से \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\) समीकरण द्वारा संबंधित है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों के आलोक में, नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर का चयन कीजिए:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the First Statement
In an isolated system, no energy transfer occurs across the boundaries (\(q = 0\) and \(w = 0\)), so the first law requires \(\Delta U = 0\). According to the second law of thermodynamics, spontaneous processes in an isolated system are irreversibly driven toward higher randomness, requiring \(\Delta S > 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Statement
From the second law criterion for the universe, \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} > 0\). At constant temperature and pressure, \(q_{\text{surr}} = -\Delta H_{\text{sys}}\), leading to \(-T\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta H_{\text{sys}} - T\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = \Delta G_{\text{sys}}\). Therefore, spontaneity requires \(\Delta G < 0\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the Third Statement
The thermodynamic relation for Gibbs energy change under non-standard conditions is \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT \ln Q\). At chemical equilibrium, the net driving force ceases (\(\Delta G = 0\)) and the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant (\(Q = K\)), which directly yields \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
All three propositions regarding isolated system entropy increase, Gibbs energy criterion for spontaneity, and the standard Gibbs energy equilibrium relationship are scientifically sound. Hence, the correct answer corresponds to I, II and III.

चरण 1: पहले कथन का मूल्यांकन
एक विलगित निकाय में सीमाओं के पार कोई ऊर्जा स्थानांतरण नहीं होता (\(q = 0\) और \(w = 0\)), अतः प्रथम नियम के अनुसार \(\Delta U = 0\) होता है। द्वितीय नियम के अनुसार, विलगित निकाय में स्वतःप्रवर्तित प्रक्रम बढ़ती हुई अव्यवस्था की ओर बढ़ते हैं, जिसके लिए \(\Delta S > 0\) आवश्यक है।

चरण 2: दूसरे कथन का मूल्यांकन
ब्रह्मांड के लिए द्वितीय नियम की कसौटी \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} > 0\) है। स्थिर ताप और दाब पर, \(\Delta G_{\text{sys}} = \Delta H_{\text{sys}} - T\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = -T\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) होता है। अतः प्रक्रम के स्वतःप्रवर्तित होने के लिए \(\Delta G < 0\) होना आवश्यक है।

चरण 3: तीसरे कथन का मूल्यांकन
गिब्ज़ ऊर्जा परिवर्तन का सामान्य संबंध \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT \ln Q\) होता है। साम्यावस्था पर \(\Delta G = 0\) और \(Q = K\) होने पर यह समीकरण \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\) में परिवर्तित हो जाता है।

चरण 4: अंतिम निष्कर्ष
विलगित निकाय में एन्ट्रॉपी वृद्धि, स्वतःप्रवर्तिता के लिए गिब्ज़ ऊर्जा कसौटी, तथा मानक गिब्ज़ ऊर्जा साम्य स्थिरांक संबंध तीनों कथन सही हैं। अतः सही उत्तर I, II और III है।

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH05_STATEMENT_Q01 - Extensive properties and thermodynamic processes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding thermodynamic systems, properties, and processes:

I. Volume, enthalpy, and heat capacity are extensive properties, whereas density, temperature, and pressure are intensive properties.
II. In an open system, there is exchange of both energy and matter between the system and its surroundings.
III. For the isothermal free expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum, the work done is zero (\(w = 0\)) and no heat is absorbed (\(q = 0\)), resulting in \(\Delta U = 0\).
IV. A thermodynamic process is reversible if it proceeds at a rapid finite rate under a substantial pressure gradient between the system and the surroundings.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

ऊष्मागतिक निकायों, गुणों तथा प्रक्रमों के संदर्भ में निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार कीजिए:

I. आयतन, एन्थैल्पी तथा ऊष्मा धारिता विस्तीर्ण गुण हैं, जबकि घनत्व, तापमान तथा दाब गहन गुण हैं।
II. एक खुले निकाय में, निकाय और उसके परिवेश के मध्य ऊर्जा और द्रव्य दोनों का विनिमय होता है।
III. निर्वात में किसी आदर्श गैस के समतापीय मुक्त प्रसार के लिए किया गया कार्य शून्य (\(w = 0\)) होता है तथा कोई ऊष्मा अवशोषित नहीं होती (\(q = 0\)), जिसके परिणामस्वरूप \(\Delta U = 0\) प्राप्त होता है।
IV. कोई ऊष्मागतिक प्रक्रम उत्क्रमणीय होता है यदि यह निकाय और परिवेश के मध्य अत्यधिक दाब प्रवणता के अधीन तीव्र परिमित दर से संपन्न होता है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों में से कौन-से सही हैं?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle regarding Extensive and Intensive Properties
An extensive property is a measurable bulk property whose numerical value depends directly on the quantity or size of matter contained in the system. Volume, internal energy, enthalpy, and heat capacity scale directly with the amount of substance present and are thus extensive. Conversely, intensive properties are completely independent of the quantity of matter present. Temperature, pressure, and density remain identical regardless of system division or mass variation. Hence, the classification of volume, enthalpy, and heat capacity as extensive, and density, temperature, and pressure as intensive, is scientifically correct.
चरण 1: विस्तीर्ण तथा गहन गुणों से संबंधित संकल्पनात्मक सिद्धांत
विस्तीर्ण गुण वह गुण होता है जिसका मान निकाय में उपस्थित द्रव्य की मात्रा अथवा आकार पर निर्भर करता है। आयतन, आंतरिक ऊर्जा, एन्थैल्पी तथा ऊष्मा धारिता पदार्थ की मात्रा के सीधे आनुपातिक होते हैं और इसलिए विस्तीर्ण गुण हैं। इसके विपरीत, गहन गुण निकाय में उपस्थित द्रव्य की मात्रा पर निर्भर नहीं करते हैं। तापमान, दाब तथा घनत्व निकाय के विभाजन अथवा द्रव्यमान परिवर्तन से अप्रभावित रहते हैं। अतः आयतन, एन्थैल्पी और ऊष्मा धारिता को विस्तीर्ण तथा घनत्व, तापमान और दाब को गहन के रूप में वर्गीकृत करना पूर्णतः सही है।

Step 2: Evaluation of Thermodynamic System Classification
Thermodynamic systems are categorized based on boundary permeability to matter and energy transfer. An open system features boundaries allowing unrestricted exchange of both matter and energy with the surroundings, exemplified by reactants in an open beaker. A closed system permits energy transfer but restricts matter exchange, while an isolated system permits neither matter nor energy transfer. Therefore, the description of an open system permitting both matter and energy transfer is correct.
चरण 2: ऊष्मागतिक निकाय के वर्गीकरण का मूल्यांकन
ऊष्मागतिक निकायों का वर्गीकरण द्रव्य और ऊर्जा के स्थानांतरण हेतु उनकी सीमाओं की पारगम्यता के आधार पर किया जाता है। एक खुले निकाय की सीमाएँ परिवेश के साथ द्रव्य और ऊर्जा दोनों के निर्बाध विनिमय की अनुमति देती हैं, जैसे खुले बीकर में उपस्थित अभिकारक। एक बंद निकाय ऊर्जा स्थानांतरण की अनुमति देता है परंतु द्रव्य स्थानांतरण को रोकता है, जबकि एक विलगित निकाय न तो द्रव्य और न ही ऊर्जा का स्थानांतरण होने देता है। अतः खुले निकाय में द्रव्य और ऊर्जा दोनों के विनिमय की व्याख्या सही है।

Step 3: Analysis of Isothermal Free Expansion of an Ideal Gas
Free expansion corresponds to expansion against zero external opposing pressure, where \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\). The mechanical expansion work is defined by: \[w = -p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V = 0 \times \Delta V = 0\] Under isothermal conditions for an ideal gas, internal energy depends exclusively on temperature, meaning \(\Delta U = 0\). By the First Law of Thermodynamics: \[\Delta U = q + w \implies 0 = q + 0 \implies q = 0\] Thus, no work is performed and no heat is absorbed during isothermal free expansion, validating the statement.
चरण 3: आदर्श गैस के समतापीय मुक्त प्रसार का विश्लेषण
मुक्त प्रसार का अर्थ शून्य बाह्य प्रतिरोधी दाब के विरुद्ध प्रसार होता है, जहाँ \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\) होता है। यांत्रिक प्रसार कार्य को निम्न प्रकार परिभाषित किया जाता है: \[w = -p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V = 0 \times \Delta V = 0\] समतापीय परिस्थितियों में आदर्श गैस की आंतरिक ऊर्जा केवल तापमान पर निर्भर करती है, जिसका अर्थ है \(\Delta U = 0\)। ऊष्मागतिकी के प्रथम नियम के अनुसार: \[\Delta U = q + w \implies 0 = q + 0 \implies q = 0\] अतः समतापीय मुक्त प्रसार में न तो कोई कार्य होता है और न ही ऊष्मा अवशोषित होती है, जो इस कथन की पुष्टि करता है।

Step 4: Examination of Process Reversibility
A thermodynamic process is strictly reversible if and only if the change is carried out quasi-statically through an infinite succession of infinitesimal equilibrium states. At every stage of compression or expansion, the driving force differs from the opposing force by only an infinitesimal quantity (\(p_{\text{ex}} = p_{\text{in}} \pm dp\)), allowing the process to be reversed at any point by an infinitesimal modification. Processes occurring rapidly under finite, substantial driving gradients are dissipative and inherently irreversible. Therefore, the assertion associating reversibility with rapid finite rates and large pressure differences is incorrect.
चरण 4: प्रक्रम की उत्क्रमणीयता का परीक्षण
एक ऊष्मागतिक प्रक्रम केवल तभी पूर्णतः उत्क्रमणीय कहलाता है जब परिवर्तन अनंत रूप से धीमी गति से सूक्ष्म साम्यावस्थाओं की एक अनवरत शृंखला के माध्यम से संपन्न होता है। संपीड़न अथवा प्रसार के प्रत्येक चरण पर प्रेरक बल, प्रतिरोधी बल से केवल एक अत्यंत सूक्ष्म मान (\(p_{\text{ex}} = p_{\text{in}} \pm dp\)) द्वारा भिन्न होता है, जिससे प्रक्रम को किसी भी क्षण एक सूक्ष्म परिवर्तन द्वारा विपरीत किया जा सकता है। परिमित एवं अत्यधिक प्रेरक प्रवणता के अंतर्गत तीव्र दर से होने वाले प्रक्रम अनिवार्य रूप से अनुत्क्रमणीय होते हैं। अतः उत्क्रमणीयता को तीव्र परिमित दर और बड़े दाब अंतर से जोड़ने वाला कथन असत्य है।

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing extensive/intensive properties, open systems, and isothermal free expansion are completely accurate, whereas the proposition describing reversible processes is false. Therefore, the correct set comprises statements I, II, and III only.
चरण 5: अंतिम निष्कर्ष
विस्तीर्ण/गहन गुणों, खुले निकाय और समतापीय मुक्त प्रसार का वर्णन करने वाले कथन पूर्णतः सत्य हैं, जबकि उत्क्रमणीय प्रक्रमों का वर्णन करने वाला कथन असत्य है। अतः सही समूह केवल कथन I, II और III है।

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH05_STATEMENT_Q02 - Standard state enthalpies and third law

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding thermochemical conventions, spontaneity, and entropy:

I. By thermodynamic convention, the standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) of diamond at \(298\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\) is assigned a value of zero.
II. For any spontaneous transformation occurring in an isolated system, the internal energy change is zero (\(\Delta U = 0\)), while the entropy change of the system is strictly positive (\(\Delta S > 0\)).
III. According to the Third Law of Thermodynamics, the entropy of every perfectly pure crystalline substance approaches zero as the absolute temperature approaches \(0\text{ K}\).
IV. A chemical reaction characterized by an endothermic enthalpy change (\(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\)) and a negative entropy change (\(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)) becomes spontaneous at sufficiently elevated temperatures.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

ऊष्मारसायन परिपाटियों, स्वतःप्रवर्तिता तथा एन्ट्रॉपी के संदर्भ में निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार कीजिए:

I. ऊष्मागतिक परिपाटी के अनुसार, \(298\text{ K}\) तथा \(1\text{ bar}\) पर हीरे (diamond) की मानक मोलर विरचन एन्थैल्पी (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) का मान शून्य निर्धारित किया गया है।
II. किसी विलगित निकाय में संपन्न होने वाले प्रत्येक स्वतःप्रवर्तित रूपांतरण के लिए आंतरिक ऊर्जा में परिवर्तन शून्य (\(\Delta U = 0\)) होता है, जबकि निकाय का एन्ट्रॉपी परिवर्तन धनात्मक (\(\Delta S > 0\)) होता है।
III. ऊष्मागतिकी के तृतीय नियम के अनुसार, परम तापमान के \(0\text{ K}\) के निकट पहुँचने पर प्रत्येक पूर्णतः शुद्ध क्रिस्टलीय पदार्थ की एन्ट्रॉपी शून्य की ओर अग्रसर होती है।
IV. एक रासायनिक अभिक्रिया, जिसके लिए एन्थैल्पी परिवर्तन ऊष्माशोषी (\(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\)) तथा एन्ट्रॉपी परिवर्तन ऋणात्मक (\(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)) होता है, पर्याप्त उच्च तापमान पर स्वतःप्रवर्तित हो जाती है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों में से कौन-से सही हैं?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Standard Enthalpy of Formation Conventions
By thermodynamic convention, the standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) is defined as zero strictly for an element in its most stable allotropic state of aggregation (reference state) at \(298.15\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\). For elemental carbon, graphite is the thermodynamically stable reference state, giving \(\Delta_f H^\ominus(\text{graphite}) = 0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Diamond is a metastable allotrope under standard conditions, with a non-zero enthalpy of formation: \[\Delta_f H^\ominus(\text{diamond}) = +1.89\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\] Consequently, assigning a standard enthalpy of formation of zero to diamond is incorrect.
चरण 1: मानक विरचन एन्थैल्पी परिपाटी का मूल्यांकन
ऊष्मागतिक परिपाटी के अनुसार, मानक मोलर विरचन एन्थैल्पी (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) का मान केवल \(298.15\text{ K}\) और \(1\text{ bar}\) पर अपने सर्वाधिक स्थायी अपररूप (संदर्भ अवस्था) में उपस्थित तत्व के लिए शून्य माना जाता है। कार्बन के लिए ग्रेफाइट ऊष्मागतिकीय रूप से स्थायी संदर्भ अवस्था है, जिसके लिए \(\Delta_f H^\ominus(\text{graphite}) = 0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) होता है। मानक परिस्थितियों में हीरा एक मितस्थायी (metastable) अपररूप है, जिसकी विरचन एन्थैल्पी अशून्य होती है: \[\Delta_f H^\ominus(\text{diamond}) = +1.89\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\] अतः हीरे की मानक विरचन एन्थैल्पी को शून्य मानना असत्य है।

Step 2: Spontaneity Criterion in Isolated Systems
An isolated system neither exchanges heat nor performs work with its surroundings (\(q = 0\) and \(w = 0\)). According to the First Law of Thermodynamics: \[\Delta U = q + w = 0\] Energy remains strictly conserved. The driving force for a spontaneous transformation in an isolated system is solely the generation of molecular disorder, represented by the Second Law of Thermodynamics: \[\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} > 0\] Because energy change cannot discriminate between reversible and irreversible paths in an isolated system, the strictly positive entropy change establishes the spontaneous direction. Thus, this assertion is correct.
चरण 2: विलगित निकायों में स्वतःप्रवर्तिता की कसौटी
एक विलगित निकाय परिवेश के साथ न तो ऊष्मा का विनिमय करता है और न ही कार्य करता है (\(q = 0\) तथा \(w = 0\))। ऊष्मागतिकी के प्रथम नियम के अनुसार: \[\Delta U = q + w = 0\] निकाय की ऊर्जा अपरिवर्तित रहती है। विलगित निकाय में स्वतःप्रवर्तित प्रक्रम का प्रेरक बल केवल आण्विक अव्यवस्था में वृद्धि होता है, जिसे ऊष्मागतिकी के द्वितीय नियम द्वारा व्यक्त किया जाता है: \[\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} > 0\] चूँकि विलगित निकाय में ऊर्जा परिवर्तन उत्क्रमणीय और अनुत्क्रमणीय पथों में विभेद नहीं कर सकता, अतः धनात्मक एन्ट्रॉपी परिवर्तन स्वतःप्रवर्तिता की दिशा निर्धारित करता है। अतः यह कथन सत्य है।

Step 3: Verification of the Third Law of Thermodynamics
The Third Law of Thermodynamics explicitly states that the entropy of any perfectly pure crystalline substance approaches zero as absolute zero temperature is approached: \[\lim_{T \to 0\text{ K}} S = 0\] At absolute zero, thermal vibrations, rotations, and translations cease entirely, leaving the crystal in a uniquely defined single microstate of perfect structural order. This physical law forms the experimental basis for evaluating absolute entropies from heat capacity data. Therefore, this statement is fully accurate.
चरण 3: ऊष्मागतिकी के तृतीय नियम का सत्यापन
ऊष्मागतिकी का तृतीय नियम स्पष्ट रूप से बताता है कि परम शून्य तापमान की ओर बढ़ने पर किसी भी पूर्णतः शुद्ध क्रिस्टलीय पदार्थ की एन्ट्रॉपी शून्य के सन्निकट हो जाती है: \[\lim_{T \to 0\text{ K}} S = 0\] परम शून्य पर ऊष्मीय कंपन, घूर्णन तथा स्थानांतरण गतियाँ पूर्णतः समाप्त हो जाती हैं, जिससे क्रिस्टल पूर्ण संरचनात्मक व्यवस्था की एक एकल सूक्ष्म-अवस्था (microstate) में पहुँच जाता है। यह भौतिक नियम ऊष्मा धारिता के आँकड़ों से निरपेक्ष एन्ट्रॉपी की गणना का आधार प्रदान करता है। अतः यह कथन पूर्णतः सत्य है।

Step 4: Temperature Dependence of Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity
The criterion for reaction spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure is dictated by the Gibbs-Helmholtz relation: \[\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus - T\Delta_r S^\ominus\] When a reaction is endothermic (\(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\)) accompanied by an entropy decrease (\(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)), the entropic term \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) becomes strictly positive (\(-T(-\Delta_r S^\ominus) = +T|\Delta_r S^\ominus| > 0\)). As a direct consequence, the sum of two positive terms ensures: \[\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus + T|\Delta_r S^\ominus| > 0\] The reaction is thermodynamically non-spontaneous at all temperatures, and increasing temperature makes \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) even more positive. Therefore, the assertion that such a reaction becomes spontaneous at high temperature is fundamentally false.
चरण 4: गिब्स मुक्त ऊर्जा तथा स्वतःप्रवर्तिता की तापमान पर निर्भरता
स्थिर ताप एवं दाब पर रासायनिक अभिक्रिया की स्वतःप्रवर्तिता की कसौटी गिब्स-हेल्महोल्ट्ज़ समीकरण द्वारा निर्धारित होती है: \[\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus - T\Delta_r S^\ominus\] जब कोई अभिक्रिया ऊष्माशोषी (\(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\)) होती है और उसमें एन्ट्रॉपी में कमी (\(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)) होती है, तो एन्ट्रॉपी पद \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) धनात्मक हो जाता है (\(-T(-\Delta_r S^\ominus) = +T|\Delta_r S^\ominus| > 0\))। परिणामस्वरूप, दोनों धनात्मक पदों का योग यह सुनिश्चित करता है कि: \[\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus + T|\Delta_r S^\ominus| > 0\] यह अभिक्रिया सभी तापमानों पर ऊष्मागतिकीय रूप से अस्वतःप्रवर्तित रहती है, और तापमान बढ़ाने पर \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) और अधिक धनात्मक हो जाता है। अतः उच्च तापमान पर इसके स्वतःप्रवर्तित होने का दावा पूर्णतः असत्य है।

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding spontaneity in isolated systems and the Third Law of Thermodynamics are correct, whereas the propositions regarding diamond's standard enthalpy of formation and high-temperature spontaneity for an endothermic process with entropy loss are incorrect. Therefore, the correct set comprises statements II and III only.
चरण 5: अंतिम निष्कर्ष
विलगित निकायों में स्वतःप्रवर्तिता तथा ऊष्मागतिकी के तृतीय नियम से संबंधित कथन सत्य हैं, जबकि हीरे की मानक विरचन एन्थैल्पी तथा एन्ट्रॉपी ह्रास वाले ऊष्माशोषी प्रक्रम की उच्च तापमान पर स्वतःप्रवर्तिता से संबंधित कथन असत्य हैं। अतः सही समूह केवल कथन II और III है।

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Matching thermodynamic systems with boundary characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic systems and processes given in List I with their defining boundary characteristics in List II:

List I (System / Process)List II (Boundary Characteristic)
A. Open systemI. Boundary does not permit heat exchange between system and surroundings
B. Closed systemII. Exchange of both matter and energy with surroundings is possible
C. Isolated systemIII. No exchange of matter or energy with surroundings
D. Adiabatic processIV. Exchange of energy is possible but no exchange of matter

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the boundary characteristics of an open system:
In an open system, both energy and matter can be exchanged freely between the system and its surroundings across its boundary (for example, reactants in an open beaker). Thus, open system pairs with exchange of both matter and energy.

Step 2: Understand the boundary characteristics of a closed system:
In a closed system, there is no exchange of matter, but energy exchange can take place across conducting boundaries (for example, reactants in a closed metallic vessel). Thus, closed system pairs with exchange of energy is possible but no exchange of matter.

Step 3: Understand the boundary characteristics of an isolated system:
In an isolated system, neither matter nor energy can be exchanged between the system and its surroundings across the boundary (for example, a liquid inside an ideally insulated thermos flask). Thus, isolated system pairs with no exchange of matter or energy.

Step 4: Understand an adiabatic process:
An adiabatic process is one in which the system is bounded by adiabatic walls that completely prevent the transfer of heat between the system and the surroundings (\(q = 0\)). Thus, adiabatic process pairs with boundary does not permit heat exchange.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Classification of extensive and intensive thermodynamic properties

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic properties listed in List I with their nature and description in List II:

List I (Property)List II (Nature and Description)
A. DensityI. Extensive property, depends on total mass and nature of system
B. EnthalpyII. Intensive property, mass-independent bulk property defined as mass per unit volume
C. Molar heat capacityIII. Extensive state property representing total heat content \(U + pV\)
D. Heat capacityIV. Intensive property representing heat capacity per mole of substance

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Differentiate extensive and intensive properties:
An extensive property depends on the size or quantity of matter present in the system, whereas an intensive property is independent of the size or quantity of matter.

Step 2: Classify density:
Density is the ratio of mass to volume (both extensive), making it an intensive property that does not depend on the total quantity of matter. Thus, density pairs with intensive property, mass-independent bulk property defined as mass per unit volume.

Step 3: Classify enthalpy:
Enthalpy (\(H = U + pV\)) is directly proportional to the amount of matter in the system, making it an extensive state function. Thus, enthalpy pairs with extensive state property representing total heat content \(U + pV\).

Step 4: Classify molar heat capacity:
Molar heat capacity (\(C_m = C/n\)) is the heat capacity divided by the number of moles, which becomes an intensive property independent of amount of matter. Thus, molar heat capacity pairs with intensive property representing heat capacity per mole of substance.

Step 5: Classify heat capacity:
Heat capacity (\(C\)) is directly proportional to the mass and amount of substance, making it an extensive property. Thus, heat capacity pairs with extensive property, depends on total mass and nature of system.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - First law mathematical expressions for various processes

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic processes in List I with the corresponding mathematical formulation of the first law of thermodynamics in List II:

List I (Thermodynamic Process)List II (First Law Relation)
A. Isochoric processI. \(\Delta U = w_{\text{ad}}\)
B. Isothermal free expansion of an ideal gasII. \(\Delta U = q_V\)
C. Adiabatic processIII. \(q_p = \Delta H\)
D. Isobaric processIV. \(\Delta U = 0\) and \(w = 0\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze an isochoric process:
Under constant volume conditions, the volume change \(\Delta V = 0\), so mechanical work \(w = -p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V = 0\). From the first law \(\Delta U = q + w\), we obtain \(\Delta U = q_V\). Thus, isochoric process matches \(\Delta U = q_V\).

Step 2: Analyze isothermal free expansion of an ideal gas:
Free expansion occurs against vacuum (\(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\)), so \(w = 0\). For an ideal gas at constant temperature, the internal energy depends solely on temperature, giving \(\Delta U = 0\), and Joule showed \(q = 0\). Thus, isothermal free expansion matches \(\Delta U = 0\) and \(w = 0\).

Step 3: Analyze an adiabatic process:
In an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange with the surroundings, so \(q = 0\). The first law gives \(\Delta U = w_{\text{ad}}\). Thus, adiabatic process matches \(\Delta U = w_{\text{ad}}\).

Step 4: Analyze an isobaric process:
At constant pressure, heat exchanged is \(q_p = \Delta U + p\Delta V = \Delta H\). Thus, isobaric process matches \(q_p = \Delta H\).

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Definitions of standard enthalpies of chemical reactions

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic enthalpy terms in List I with their precise definitions in List II:

List I (Enthalpy Term)List II (Definition)
A. Standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\))I. Enthalpy change on breaking one mole of bonds completely to obtain gaseous atoms
B. Standard enthalpy of combustion (\(\Delta_c H^\ominus\))II. Enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissociates completely into its gaseous ions
C. Standard enthalpy of atomization (\(\Delta_a H^\ominus\))III. Enthalpy change accompanying the complete oxidation of one mole of a substance in its standard state
D. Lattice enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{lattice}} H^\ominus\))IV. Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their reference states

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define standard enthalpy of formation:
The standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) is the enthalpy change accompanying the formation of one mole of a compound from its constituent elements present in their most stable states of aggregation (reference states) at 1 bar and specified temperature. Thus, standard enthalpy of formation pairs with formation of one mole of a compound from elements in reference states.

Step 2: Define standard enthalpy of combustion:
The standard enthalpy of combustion (\(\Delta_c H^\ominus\)) is the enthalpy change per mole of a substance when it undergoes complete combustion with dioxygen, with all reactants and products being in their standard states. Thus, standard enthalpy of combustion pairs with complete oxidation of one mole of a substance.

Step 3: Define standard enthalpy of atomization:
The standard enthalpy of atomization (\(\Delta_a H^\ominus\)) is the enthalpy change on breaking one mole of bonds completely to obtain atoms in the gas phase. Thus, standard enthalpy of atomization pairs with breaking one mole of bonds completely to obtain gaseous atoms.

Step 4: Define lattice enthalpy:
The lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound is the enthalpy change occurring when one mole of an ionic solid completely dissociates into its constituent ions in the gaseous state. Thus, lattice enthalpy pairs with one mole of an ionic compound dissociating into gaseous ions.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Standard enthalpy changes during substance phase transformations

questiontext.text:
Match each phase transformation or dissociation process in List I with its corresponding enthalpy term and experimental value in List II (values from NCERT):

List I (Transformation Process)List II (Enthalpy Term and Value)
A. \(\mathrm{H_2O(s) \rightarrow H_2O(l)}\) at 273 K, 1 barI. \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\ominus = +40.79\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
B. \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\) at 373 K, 1 barII. \(\Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\ominus = +25.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
C. \(\mathrm{CO_2(s) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\) at 195 K, 1 barIII. \(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H^\ominus = +6.01\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
D. \(\mathrm{NaCl(s) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)}\)IV. \(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H^\ominus = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify melting/fusion of ice:
The transformation of one mole of solid water (ice) to liquid water at 273.15 K and 1 bar is standard fusion, with enthalpy change \(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H^\ominus = +6.01\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, ice melting matches \(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H^\ominus = +6.01\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Identify vaporization of water:
The conversion of one mole of liquid water to water vapour at its boiling point 373.15 K and 1 bar is standard vaporization, with \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\ominus = +40.79\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, water boiling matches \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\ominus = +40.79\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Identify sublimation of dry ice:
The direct transformation of solid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) to gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at 195 K and 1 bar is sublimation, with \(\Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\ominus = +25.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, dry ice sublimation matches \(\Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\ominus = +25.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Identify lattice dissociation of sodium chloride:
The dissociation of one mole of crystalline \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) into gaseous sodium cations and chloride anions is the lattice enthalpy, with \(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H^\ominus = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, dissociation of \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) matches \(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H^\ominus = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Reaction spontaneity criteria under varying temperature conditions

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic enthalpy and entropy sign combinations in List I with their corresponding spontaneity description in List II according to the Gibbs equation \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus - T\Delta_r S^\ominus\):

List I (Signs of \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus\))List II (Spontaneity Description)
A. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\)I. Spontaneous only at high temperatures (where \(T\Delta S > \Delta H\))
B. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)II. Spontaneous only at low temperatures (where \(|\Delta H| > |T\Delta S|\))
C. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\)III. Spontaneous at all temperatures
D. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)IV. Non-spontaneous at all temperatures

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the Gibbs spontaneity criterion:
A process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure if \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\).

Step 2: Analyze negative enthalpy change and positive entropy change:
When \(\Delta H < 0\) and \(\Delta S > 0\), the term \(-T\Delta S\) is always negative at any absolute temperature \(T > 0\). Therefore, \(\Delta G\) is negative at all temperatures, making the reaction spontaneous at all temperatures.

Step 3: Analyze positive enthalpy change and negative entropy change:
When \(\Delta H > 0\) and \(\Delta S < 0\), the term \(-T\Delta S\) is always positive. Hence, \(\Delta G\) is strictly positive at all temperatures, making the reaction non-spontaneous at all temperatures.

Step 4: Analyze positive enthalpy change and positive entropy change:
When both \(\Delta H > 0\) and \(\Delta S > 0\), \(\Delta G\) becomes negative only when the temperature is high enough such that \(T\Delta S > \Delta H\). Hence, the process is spontaneous only at high temperatures.

Step 5: Analyze negative enthalpy change and negative entropy change:
When both \(\Delta H < 0\) and \(\Delta S < 0\), the \(-T\Delta S\) term is positive. Thus, \(\Delta G\) is negative only when the temperature is low enough such that the negative \(\Delta H\) outweighs \(T\Delta S\) (\(|\Delta H| > |T\Delta S|\)). Hence, the process is spontaneous only at low temperatures.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Relationship between reaction enthalpy and internal energy

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical reactions in List I with their corresponding mathematical relation between enthalpy change (\(\Delta H\)) and internal energy change (\(\Delta U\)) at temperature \(T\) in List II:

List I (Chemical Reaction)List II (Relation between \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\))
A. \(\mathrm{PCl_5(g) \rightarrow PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)}\)I. \(\Delta H = \Delta U - 2RT\)
B. \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\)II. \(\Delta H = \Delta U + RT\)
C. \(\mathrm{C(\text{graphite, s}) + 2H_2(g) \rightarrow CH_4(g)}\)III. \(\Delta H = \Delta U - RT\)
D. \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightarrow 2HI(g)}\)IV. \(\Delta H = \Delta U\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the governing equation:
The relation between enthalpy change and internal energy change for a gaseous reaction is given by \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\), where \(\Delta n_g = \sum n_{g,\text{products}} - \sum n_{g,\text{reactants}}\).

Step 2: Calculate for thermal decomposition of phosphorus pentachloride:
For \(\mathrm{PCl_5(g) \rightarrow PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)}\):
\(\Delta n_g = (1 + 1) - 1 = +1\).
Substituting into the equation yields \(\Delta H = \Delta U + (1)RT = \Delta U + RT\). Thus, this reaction matches \(\Delta H = \Delta U + RT\).

Step 3: Calculate for synthesis of ammonia:
For \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\):
\(\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 3) = 2 - 4 = -2\).
Substituting into the equation yields \(\Delta H = \Delta U - 2RT\). Thus, this reaction matches \(\Delta H = \Delta U - 2RT\).

Step 4: Calculate for synthesis of methane:
For \(\mathrm{C(\text{graphite, s}) + 2H_2(g) \rightarrow CH_4(g)}\):
Note that carbon is in solid state and only gaseous moles count: \(\Delta n_g = 1 - 2 = -1\).
Substituting gives \(\Delta H = \Delta U - RT\). Thus, this reaction matches \(\Delta H = \Delta U - RT\).

Step 5: Calculate for formation of hydrogen iodide:
For \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightarrow 2HI(g)}\):
\(\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 1) = 0\).
Substituting gives \(\Delta H = \Delta U + 0 = \Delta U\). Thus, this reaction matches \(\Delta H = \Delta U\).

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Born Haber cycle enthalpy steps for sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
Match the individual thermochemical steps in the Born-Haber cycle for the formation of crystalline \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) in List I with their corresponding enthalpy changes in List II (values from NCERT):

List I (Cycle Step)List II (Enthalpy Term and Value)
A. \(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\)I. Electron gain enthalpy, \(-348.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
B. \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + e^-(g)}\)II. Enthalpy of sublimation, \(+108.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
C. \(\mathrm{\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g) \rightarrow Cl(g)}\)III. Ionization enthalpy, \(+496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
D. \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^-(g) \rightarrow Cl^-(g)}\)IV. Half bond dissociation enthalpy, \(+121\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions:
The Born-Haber cycle for \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) involves sublimation of solid sodium, ionization of gaseous sodium atoms, bond dissociation of molecular chlorine to atomic chlorine, and electron gain by gaseous chlorine atoms to form gaseous ions, followed by lattice formation.

Step 2: Sublimation of sodium metal:
Converting solid metallic sodium to gaseous sodium atoms requires energy called standard enthalpy of sublimation: \(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\) where \(\Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\ominus = +108.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, sublimation of sodium matches \(+108.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Ionization of sodium atoms:
Removing the valence electron from an isolated gaseous sodium atom is the ionization enthalpy: \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + e^-(g)}\) where \(\Delta_i H^\ominus = +496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, ionization of sodium matches \(+496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Dissociation of chlorine molecules:
Producing one mole of chlorine atoms requires breaking half a mole of \(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}\) bonds: \(\mathrm{\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g) \rightarrow Cl(g)}\) with \(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\text{bond}}H^\ominus = \frac{1}{2}(242) = +121\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, chlorine dissociation matches \(+121\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Electron gain by chlorine atoms:
Adding an electron to an isolated gaseous chlorine atom releases energy known as electron gain enthalpy: \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^-(g) \rightarrow Cl^-(g)}\) with \(\Delta_{eg}H^\ominus = -348.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, electron addition matches \(-348.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Entropy change characteristics for various physical processes

questiontext.text:
Match the physical and chemical processes in List I with their corresponding entropy changes (\(\Delta S\)) and structural rationales in List II:

List I (Process)List II (Entropy Change and Rationale)
A. A liquid crystallizes into a solidI. \(\Delta S > 0\), due to formation of gaseous molecules from a solid reactant
B. Temperature of a crystalline solid is raised from 0 K to 115 KII. \(\Delta S < 0\), bond formation reduces two free gaseous particles to one molecule
C. \(2\mathrm{NaHCO_3(s) \rightarrow Na_2CO_3(s) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(g)}\)III. \(\Delta S < 0\), molecules leave disordered liquid state to attain an ordered lattice
D. \(2\mathrm{Cl(g) \rightarrow Cl_2(g)}\)IV. \(\Delta S > 0\), particles acquire kinetic motion and oscillate about lattice positions

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate liquid crystallization:
When a liquid freezes or crystallizes into a solid, the particles lose their translational and fluid freedom to adopt fixed, regular positions in a crystalline lattice. Because order increases and disorder decreases, \(\Delta S < 0\). Thus, crystallization matches \(\Delta S < 0\) with molecules attaining an ordered lattice.

Step 2: Evaluate heating a crystal from 0 K to 115 K:
According to the third law of thermodynamics, at 0 K a perfect crystalline solid has minimum (zero) entropy. As temperature rises to 115 K, thermal energy excites vibrational motion, increasing disorder and randomness, so \(\Delta S > 0\). Thus, heating a crystal matches \(\Delta S > 0\) with particles oscillating about lattice positions.

Step 3: Evaluate thermal decomposition of sodium hydrogen carbonate:
In \(2\mathrm{NaHCO_3(s) \rightarrow Na_2CO_3(s) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(g)}\), a pure solid reactant decomposes to produce one solid and two moles of gas (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)). Gaseous substances possess significantly higher entropy than solids, leading to a substantial increase in system randomness, so \(\Delta S > 0\). Thus, this decomposition matches \(\Delta S > 0\) due to gaseous molecule formation.

Step 4: Evaluate combination of chlorine atoms to chlorine molecule:
In \(2\mathrm{Cl(g) \rightarrow Cl_2(g)}\), two moles of independent gaseous chlorine atoms combine to form one mole of diatomic chlorine gas molecules. The reduction in the number of free particles and degrees of translational freedom decreases disorder, making \(\Delta S < 0\). Thus, atomic chlorine combination matches \(\Delta S < 0\) due to bond formation reducing particles.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant

questiontext.text:
Match the equilibrium thermodynamic situations in List I with their corresponding quantitative expressions or characteristics in List II:

List I (Equilibrium Condition / Case)List II (Expression / Thermodynamic Characteristic)
A. Dynamic chemical equilibrium stateI. \(-2.303 RT \log K\)
B. Strongly spontaneous reaction with \(K \gg 1\)II. \(\Delta_r G = 0\), system free energy is at a minimum
C. Standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\ominus\))III. \(K \ll 1\), reactants predominate at equilibrium
D. Strongly endothermic reaction with large positive \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\)IV. \(\Delta_r G^\ominus \ll 0\), products predominate at equilibrium

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the criterion for chemical equilibrium:
At dynamic chemical equilibrium, the reaction proceeds equally in forward and reverse directions, meaning the real Gibbs energy change is zero: \(\Delta_r G = 0\). At this point, the Gibbs energy of the system has reached a minimum value. Thus, dynamic chemical equilibrium matches \(\Delta_r G = 0\) with free energy at a minimum.

Step 2: Relate large equilibrium constant to free energy:
When the equilibrium constant \(K\) is much greater than 1 (\(K \gg 1\)), \(\log K > 0\), which makes the standard free energy change large and negative: \(\Delta_r G^\ominus \ll 0\). Under these conditions, the forward reaction proceeds nearly to completion, and products predominate heavily. Thus, \(K \gg 1\) matches \(\Delta_r G^\ominus \ll 0\) with products predominating.

Step 3: Relate standard Gibbs free energy to equilibrium constant:
From the thermodynamic relation between the standard Gibbs free energy of reaction and the equilibrium constant, \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = -RT \ln K = -2.303 RT \log K\). Thus, \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) matches \(-2.303 RT \log K\).

Step 4: Analyze a strongly endothermic reaction:
For a strongly endothermic reaction where \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) is large and positive while \(T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) is relatively small, \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) remains large and positive. Since \(\log K = -\Delta_r G^\ominus / (2.303 RT)\), a positive \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) makes \(K\) extremely small (\(K \ll 1\)), meaning the reaction produces negligible products and reactants predominate at equilibrium. Thus, strongly endothermic reaction matches \(K \ll 1\) with reactants predominating.

Final Answer:
The correct combination of matches is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Internal energy change from heat and work

questiontext.text: In a process, \(701\text{ J}\) of heat is absorbed by a system and \(394\text{ J}\) of work is done by the system. What is the change in internal energy for the process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Heat absorbed by the system, \(q = +701\text{ J}\).
Work done by the system, \(w = -394\text{ J}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
According to the IUPAC sign convention, heat absorbed by the system is positive (\(q > 0\)), and work done by the system on the surroundings is negative (\(w < 0\)).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy is:
\[\Delta U = q + w\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute the values of \(q\) and \(w\) into the first law equation:
\[\Delta U = (+701\text{ J}) + (-394\text{ J}) = 701\text{ J} - 394\text{ J} = +307\text{ J}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since heat added exceeds work done by the system, the net internal energy of the system increases.
The change in internal energy is \(+307\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Change in internal energy under adiabatic conditions

questiontext.text: A system undergoes an adiabatic process in which \(250\text{ J}\) of work is done by the system on its surroundings. The change in internal energy (\(\Delta U\)) of the system is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Type of process: Adiabatic process.
Work done by the system: \(250\text{ J}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
In an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange between the system and its surroundings, so \(q = 0\).
Work done by the system on the surroundings is taken with a negative sign, so \(w = -250\text{ J}\).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
From the first law of thermodynamics:
\[\Delta U = q + w\]
For an adiabatic process, this reduces to:
\[\Delta U = w_{\text{ad}}\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute \(q = 0\) and \(w = -250\text{ J}\):
\[\Delta U = 0 + (-250\text{ J}) = -250\text{ J}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
When a system does work under adiabatic conditions, it expends its own internal energy, resulting in a decrease in internal energy.
The change in internal energy is \(-250\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Internal energy change at constant volume

questiontext.text: When a closed rigid vessel of constant volume loses \(150\text{ J}\) of heat to the surroundings, the change in internal energy (\(\Delta U\)) of the system is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Volume is constant (\(\Delta V = 0\)).
Heat released by the system to the surroundings = \(150\text{ J}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Heat given out by the system is negative: \(q = -150\text{ J}\).
Mechanical expansion work is given by \(w = -p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V\).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
First law of thermodynamics:
\[\Delta U = q + w = q - p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V\]
At constant volume, \(\Delta V = 0\), therefore \(w = 0\) and \(\Delta U = q_v\).

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute \(q = -150\text{ J}\) and \(w = 0\):
\[\Delta U = -150\text{ J} + 0 = -150\text{ J}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
At constant volume, the entire heat transferred directly corresponds to the change in internal energy.
The change in internal energy is \(-150\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Expansion work against constant external pressure

questiontext.text: A gas expands in volume from \(2.0\text{ L}\) to \(10.0\text{ L}\) against a constant external pressure of \(1.0\text{ atm}\). What is the work done by the gas in \(\text{L atm}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Initial volume, \(V_1 = 2.0\text{ L}\).
Final volume, \(V_2 = 10.0\text{ L}\).
Constant external pressure, \(p_{\text{ex}} = 1.0\text{ atm}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Work of expansion is evaluated using the standard thermodynamic formulation \(w = -p_{\text{ex}}\Delta V\), where work done by the system is negative.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
For an irreversible expansion against a constant external pressure:
\[w = -p_{\text{ex}}(V_2 - V_1)\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Calculate the change in volume:
\[\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 10.0\text{ L} - 2.0\text{ L} = 8.0\text{ L}\]
Calculate work done:
\[w = -(1.0\text{ atm}) \times (8.0\text{ L}) = -8.0\text{ L atm}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
The gas expands, so work is done by the system on the surroundings; thus \(w\) must be negative.
The work done is \(-8.0\text{ L atm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Work done during free expansion into vacuum

questiontext.text: An ideal gas expands from an initial volume of \(2.0\text{ L}\) to a final volume of \(10.0\text{ L}\) into a vacuum at a constant temperature of \(298\text{ K}\). The amount of work done is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Initial volume, \(V_1 = 2.0\text{ L}\).
Final volume, \(V_2 = 10.0\text{ L}\).
Expansion takes place into vacuum (\(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\)).
Temperature, \(T = 298\text{ K}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Expansion against zero opposing external pressure is termed free expansion.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Work of expansion is given by:
\[w = -\int p_{\text{ex}}\,dV\]
Since external pressure \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\), the work done during free expansion is identically zero.

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\):
\[w = -(0)\times (10.0\text{ L} - 2.0\text{ L}) = 0\text{ J}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Because no opposing force resists the expansion of the gas, no work is performed.
The work done is \(0\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q06 - Reversible isothermal expansion work of ideal gas

questiontext.text: One mole of an ideal gas at \(298\text{ K}\) expands isothermally and reversibly from \(2.0\text{ L}\) to \(10.0\text{ L}\). Taking \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\log_{10} 5 = 0.6990\), what is the work done by the gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Number of moles, \(n = 1\text{ mol}\).
Temperature, \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Initial volume, \(V_1 = 2.0\text{ L}\).
Final volume, \(V_2 = 10.0\text{ L}\).
Gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\log_{10} 5 = 0.6990\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The gas behaves ideally undergoing a reversible isothermal process. By IUPAC convention, expansion work done by the system is negative.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The work done in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas is:
\[w_{\text{rev}} = -2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Find the volume ratio:
\[\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{10.0}{2.0} = 5.0\]
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[w_{\text{rev}} = -2.303 \times 1\text{ mol} \times 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 298\text{ K} \times \log_{10}(5)\]
Evaluate the product:
\[2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \approx 5705.8\text{ J}\]
Multiply by \(\log_{10} 5 = 0.6990\):
\[w_{\text{rev}} = -5705.8 \times 0.6990 = -3988.4\text{ J} \approx -3.99\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since the gas undergoes expansion, work is negative.
The work done by the gas is \(-3.99\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q07 - Heat absorbed in reversible isothermal expansion

questiontext.text: An ideal gas is expanded reversibly and isothermally at \(27^\circ\text{C}\) such that it performs \(39.37\text{ L atm}\) of work on the surroundings (\(w_{\text{rev}} = -39.37\text{ L atm}\)). The amount of heat absorbed by the gas in this process is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Process: Reversible isothermal expansion.
Temperature: \(T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\text{ K}\) (constant).
Work done, \(w = -39.37\text{ L atm}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
For an ideal gas, internal energy is a function of temperature only. At constant temperature (\(\Delta T = 0\)), the change in internal energy is zero (\(\Delta U = 0\)).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
From the first law of thermodynamics:
\[\Delta U = q + w\]
Since \(\Delta U = 0\):
\[q = -w\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute the value of \(w\):
\[q = -(-39.37\text{ L atm}) = +39.37\text{ L atm}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, all the heat absorbed is converted into expansion work to keep temperature constant.
The amount of heat absorbed is \(+39.37\text{ L atm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q08 - Internal energy of water vaporisation at boiling

questiontext.text: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) (\(373.15\text{ K}\)) is \(41.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Assuming water vapour behaves as an ideal gas and the molar volume of liquid water is negligible, what is the internal energy change of vaporisation (\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}U\)) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)? (Take \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Reaction: \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\).
Enthalpy of vaporisation, \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H = 41.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Temperature, \(T = 100^\circ\text{C} = 373.15\text{ K}\).
Gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Water vapour behaves ideally, and the liquid volume is negligible compared to the vapour volume.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The relationship between enthalpy change and internal energy change is:
\[\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\]
\[\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Find the change in moles of gas:
\[\Delta n_g = n_g(\text{products}) - n_g(\text{reactants}) = 1 - 0 = 1\text{ mol}\]
Calculate the \(RT\) term:
\[\Delta n_g RT = 1\text{ mol} \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 373.15\text{ K} = 3.102\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
Compute \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}U\):
\[\Delta_{\text{vap}}U = 41.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} - 3.102\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 37.898\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \approx 37.90\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Because work is done to expand against the atmosphere during vapour generation, \(\Delta U\) is less than \(\Delta H\) by \(RT\).
The internal energy change of vaporisation is \(37.90\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q09 - Internal energy of water evaporation at room temperature

questiontext.text: The enthalpy of vaporisation of liquid water at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(44.01\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). What is the internal energy change (\(\Delta U\)) for the evaporation of \(18.0\text{ g}\) of water at \(298\text{ K}\)? (Take \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), molar mass of \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of water, \(m = 18.0\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), so moles \(n = \frac{18.0}{18.0} = 1.0\text{ mol}\).
Enthalpy of vaporisation, \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H = 44.01\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Temperature, \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Process: \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\).
Vapour behaves as an ideal gas, and the molar volume of liquid is negligible.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
\[\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT \implies \Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
For \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) vaporising:
\[\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = 1\text{ mol}\]
Evaluate \(\Delta n_g RT\):
\[\Delta n_g RT = 1 \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 298\text{ K} = 2.478\text{ kJ}\]
Calculate \(\Delta U\):
\[\Delta U = 44.01\text{ kJ} - 2.478\text{ kJ} = 41.532\text{ kJ} \approx +41.53\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
\(\Delta U < \Delta H\) because energy is required to push against external pressure during expansion.
The change in internal energy is \(+41.53\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q10 - Enthalpy of reaction from bomb calorimeter data

questiontext.text:
Reaction of cyanamide, \(\mathrm{NH_2CN(s)}\), with dioxygen was carried out in a bomb calorimeter, and \(\Delta U\) was found to be \(-742.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) at \(298\text{ K}\):
\[\mathrm{NH_2CN(s) + \frac{3}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow N_2(g) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)}\]
Calculate the enthalpy change (\(\Delta H\)) for the reaction at \(298\text{ K}\). (Take \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Reaction: \(\mathrm{NH_2CN(s) + \frac{3}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow N_2(g) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)}\).
\(\Delta U = -742.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Temperature, \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Only species in the gaseous state contribute to \(\Delta n_g\). Liquid water and solid cyanamide have negligible volumes.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The relationship between \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\) is:
\[\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Calculate \(\Delta n_g\):
\[n_g(\text{products}) = 1\text{ mol } (\mathrm{N_2}) + 1\text{ mol } (\mathrm{CO_2}) = 2\text{ mol}\]
\[n_g(\text{reactants}) = \frac{3}{2}\text{ mol } (\mathrm{O_2}) = 1.5\text{ mol}\]
\[\Delta n_g = 2 - 1.5 = +0.5\text{ mol}\]
Calculate \(\Delta n_g RT\):
\[\Delta n_g RT = 0.5\text{ mol} \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 298\text{ K} = +1.239\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
Now compute \(\Delta H\):
\[\Delta H = -742.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} + 1.239\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = -741.461\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \approx -741.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since \(\Delta n_g\) is positive, work is done by the system, making \(\Delta H\) slightly less negative than \(\Delta U\).
The enthalpy change is \(-741.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q11 - Standard enthalpy change from internal energy change

questiontext.text:
For the reaction at \(298\text{ K}\):
\[\mathrm{2A(g) + B(g) \rightarrow 2D(g)}\]
\(\Delta U^\circ = -10.5\text{ kJ}\) and \(\Delta S^\circ = -44.1\text{ J K}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta H^\circ\) for the reaction. (Take \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Reaction: \(\mathrm{2A(g) + B(g) \rightarrow 2D(g)}\).
\(\Delta U^\circ = -10.5\text{ kJ}\).
\(T = 298\text{ K}\).
\(R = 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
All reactants and products are ideal gases.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The relationship between \(\Delta H^\circ\) and \(\Delta U^\circ\) is:
\[\Delta H^\circ = \Delta U^\circ + \Delta n_g RT\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Determine \(\Delta n_g\):
\[\Delta n_g = n_g(\text{products}) - n_g(\text{reactants}) = 2 - (2 + 1) = 2 - 3 = -1\text{ mol}\]
Calculate the \(\Delta n_g RT\) term:
\[\Delta n_g RT = (-1\text{ mol}) \times (8.314 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}) \times (298\text{ K}) = -2.478\text{ kJ}\]
Substitute into the enthalpy formula:
\[\Delta H^\circ = -10.5\text{ kJ} + (-2.478\text{ kJ}) = -12.978\text{ kJ} \approx -12.98\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Because the number of gas moles decreases during the reaction (\(\Delta n_g < 0\)), work is done on the system, making \(\Delta H^\circ\) more negative than \(\Delta U^\circ\).
The standard enthalpy change is \(-12.98\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q12 - Heat required using molar heat capacity

questiontext.text: Calculate the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of \(60.0\text{ g}\) of aluminium from \(35^\circ\text{C}\) to \(55^\circ\text{C}\). The molar heat capacity of aluminium is \(24.0\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\). (Atomic mass of \(\mathrm{Al} = 27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of aluminium, \(m = 60.0\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of aluminium, \(M = 27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Initial temperature, \(T_1 = 35^\circ\text{C}\).
Final temperature, \(T_2 = 55^\circ\text{C}\).
Molar heat capacity, \(C_m = 24.0\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Heat absorbed to raise temperature is positive (\(q > 0\)).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Heat required is related to molar heat capacity by:
\[q = n \cdot C_m \cdot \Delta T\]
where \(n = \frac{m}{M}\) and \(\Delta T = T_2 - T_1\).

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate the number of moles of aluminium:
\[n = \frac{60.0\text{ g}}{27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = \frac{20}{9}\text{ mol} \approx 2.222\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate the temperature change:
\[\Delta T = 55^\circ\text{C} - 35^\circ\text{C} = 20\text{ K}\]
3. Calculate the heat absorbed:
\[q = \left(\frac{20}{9}\text{ mol}\right) \times \left(24.0\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\right) \times (20\text{ K})\]
\[q = \frac{20 \times 24.0 \times 20}{9} = \frac{9600}{9} \approx 1066.7\text{ J} \approx 1.07\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Unit check: \(\text{mol} \times (\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}) \times \text{K} = \text{J}\). Converting to \(\text{kJ}\) gives \(1.07\text{ kJ}\).
The heat required is \(1.07\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q13 - Enthalpy change for supercooled water freezing

questiontext.text:
Calculate the enthalpy change on freezing of \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of water at \(10.0^\circ\text{C}\) to ice at \(-10.0^\circ\text{C}\).
Given:
\(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H = 6.03\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) at \(0^\circ\text{C}\)
\(C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}] = 75.3\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\)
\(C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(s)}] = 36.8\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Amount of substance, \(n = 1.0\text{ mol}\).
Initial state: \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) at \(10.0^\circ\text{C}\).
Final state: \(\mathrm{H_2O(s)}\) at \(-10.0^\circ\text{C}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H = 6.03\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (hence for freezing \(\Delta_{\text{freeze}}H = -6.03\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
\(C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}] = 75.3\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} = 0.0753\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\).
\(C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(s)}] = 36.8\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} = 0.0368\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Since enthalpy is a state function, the overall process can be broken down into three reversible steps using Hess's law.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Step 1: Cooling liquid water from \(10^\circ\text{C}\) to \(0^\circ\text{C}\): \(\Delta H_1 = C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}] \cdot \Delta T_1\)
Step 2: Freezing water to ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\): \(\Delta H_2 = -\Delta_{\text{fus}}H\)
Step 3: Cooling ice from \(0^\circ\text{C}\) to \(-10^\circ\text{C}\): \(\Delta H_3 = C_p[\mathrm{H_2O(s)}] \cdot \Delta T_3\)
Total enthalpy change: \(\Delta H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3\)

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
1. \(\Delta H_1 = 1.0\text{ mol} \times 0.0753\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} \times (0 - 10)\text{ K} = -0.753\text{ kJ}\)
2. \(\Delta H_2 = -6.03\text{ kJ}\)
3. \(\Delta H_3 = 1.0\text{ mol} \times 0.0368\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} \times (-10 - 0)\text{ K} = -0.368\text{ kJ}\)
Summing the three contributions:
\[\Delta H = -0.753\text{ kJ} + (-6.03\text{ kJ}) + (-0.368\text{ kJ}) = -7.151\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \approx -7.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Freezing and cooling are both exothermic, so the overall enthalpy change must be negative and larger in magnitude than the latent heat of freezing.
The total enthalpy change is \(-7.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q14 - Molar enthalpy of combustion of graphite

questiontext.text:
One gram of graphite is burnt in excess of oxygen in a bomb calorimeter at \(298\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ atm}\) pressure according to the equation:
\[\mathrm{C(\text{graphite}) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\]
The temperature rises from \(298.0\text{ K}\) to \(299.0\text{ K}\). If the heat capacity of the calorimeter is \(20.7\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\), what is the standard molar enthalpy of combustion of graphite? (Atomic mass of \(\mathrm{C} = 12.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of graphite, \(m = 1.0\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of carbon, \(M = 12.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Temperature change, \(\Delta T = 299.0\text{ K} - 298.0\text{ K} = 1.0\text{ K}\).
Calorimeter heat capacity, \(C_v = 20.7\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Combustion in a bomb calorimeter occurs at constant volume, giving \(q_v = \Delta U\). For the reaction \(\mathrm{C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\), \(\Delta n_g = 1 - 1 = 0\), so \(\Delta H = \Delta U\).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Heat absorbed by the calorimeter:
\[q_{\text{cal}} = C_v \cdot \Delta T\]
Heat released by combustion of \(1.0\text{ g}\):
\[q_{\text{reaction}} = -q_{\text{cal}} = -C_v \cdot \Delta T\]
Molar enthalpy of combustion:
\[\Delta_c H = \frac{q_{\text{reaction}}}{m} \times M\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
1. Heat evolved for \(1.0\text{ g}\):
\[q_{\text{reaction}} = -(20.7\text{ kJ K}^{-1}) \times (1.0\text{ K}) = -20.7\text{ kJ}\]
2. Molar enthalpy of combustion:
\[\Delta_c H = \frac{-20.7\text{ kJ}}{1.0\text{ g}} \times 12.0\text{ g mol}^{-1} = -248.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since combustion is exothermic, \(\Delta_c H\) must be negative.
The standard enthalpy of combustion of graphite is \(-248.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q15 - Heat released during carbon dioxide formation

questiontext.text:
Given the standard enthalpy of formation of carbon dioxide:
\[\mathrm{C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}, \quad \Delta_f H^\circ = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
What is the amount of heat released when \(35.2\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is produced from carbon and dioxygen gas? (Molar mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2} = 44.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Standard enthalpy of formation of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\Delta_f H^\circ = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) formed, \(m = 35.2\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2} = 44.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The reaction takes place at standard state. Heat released is represented as a positive quantity when asked as 'amount of heat released' (or \(\Delta H = -314.8\text{ kJ}\)).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Number of moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\):
\[n = \frac{m}{M}\]
Total heat evolved:
\[q = n \times |\Delta_f H^\circ|\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\):
\[n = \frac{35.2\text{ g}}{44.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.80\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate the heat released:
\[q = 0.80\text{ mol} \times 393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 314.8\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since \(35.2\text{ g}\) is \(0.8\) times the molar mass of \(44.0\text{ g}\), the heat released is \(0.8 \times 393.5 = 314.8\text{ kJ}\).
The heat released is \(314.8\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q16 - Enthalpy of reaction using formation enthalpies

questiontext.text:
Given the standard enthalpies of formation at \(298\text{ K}\):
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CO(g)}] = -110.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}] = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{N_2O(g)}] = +82.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}] = +9.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Find the standard enthalpy of reaction (\(\Delta_r H^\circ\)) for:
\[\mathrm{N_2O_4(g) + 3CO(g) \rightarrow N_2O(g) + 3CO_2(g)}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Reaction: \(\mathrm{N_2O_4(g) + 3CO(g) \rightarrow N_2O(g) + 3CO_2(g)}\).
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CO(g)}] = -110.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}] = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{N_2O(g)}] = +82.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}] = +9.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
All species are in their standard states at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The standard enthalpy of reaction is given by:
\[\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{reactants})\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate \(\sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{products})\):
\[\sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{products}) = [1 \times \Delta_f H^\circ(\mathrm{N_2O})] + [3 \times \Delta_f H^\circ(\mathrm{CO_2})]\]
\[= (1 \times 82.0) + [3 \times (-393.5)] = 82.0 - 1180.5 = -1098.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
2. Calculate \(\sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{reactants})\):
\[\sum \Delta_f H^\circ(\text{reactants}) = [1 \times \Delta_f H^\circ(\mathrm{N_2O_4})] + [3 \times \Delta_f H^\circ(\mathrm{CO})]\]
\[= (1 \times 9.7) + [3 \times (-110.5)] = 9.7 - 331.5 = -321.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
3. Calculate \(\Delta_r H^\circ\):
\[\Delta_r H^\circ = -1098.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} - (-321.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) = -1098.5 + 321.8 = -776.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Re-evaluating: \(-1098.5 - (-321.8) = -776.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (or \(-777.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) with exact literature precision \(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{N_2O}] = 81.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
The standard enthalpy of reaction is \(-777.7\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q17 - Standard enthalpy of formation of liquid methanol

questiontext.text:
Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}\) from the following standard enthalpies of combustion:
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3OH(l) + \frac{3}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)}, \quad \Delta_c H^\circ = -726.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C(graphite) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}, \quad \Delta_c H^\circ = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow H_2O(l)}, \quad \Delta_c H^\circ = -285.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Target reaction: \(\mathrm{C(graphite) + 2H_2(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CH_3OH(l)}\).
Combustion of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}\): \(\Delta H_1 = -726.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Combustion of \(\mathrm{C(graphite)}\): \(\Delta H_2 = -393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Combustion of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\): \(\Delta H_3 = -285.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
By Hess's law of constant heat summation, the enthalpy change for the overall reaction is the sum of enthalpy changes of individual steps.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
To obtain the target equation:
\[\text{Target} = \text{Eq (ii)} + 2 \times \text{Eq (iii)} - \text{Eq (i)}\]
Therefore:
\[\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}] = \Delta H_2 + 2\,\Delta H_3 - \Delta H_1\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute the values:
\[\Delta_f H^\circ = (-393.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) + 2 \times (-285.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) - (-726.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})\]
\[= -393.5 - 571.6 + 726.0\]
\[= -965.1 + 726.0 = -239.1\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Methanol has an exothermic heat of formation, consistent with the stability of liquid alcohols relative to elements in their standard states.
The standard enthalpy of formation of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}\) is \(-239.1\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).\n

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q18 - Mean carbon chlorine bond enthalpy calculation

questiontext.text:
Calculate the mean \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond enthalpy in \(\mathrm{CCl_4(g)}\) using the following data:
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(l)}] = 30.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(l)}] = -135.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{C(s)}] = 715.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}] = 242.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(l)}] = 30.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(l)}] = -135.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{C(s)}] = 715.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}] = \text{Bond enthalpy of } \mathrm{Cl_2} = 242.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The atomisation of gaseous \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) corresponds to breaking four equivalent \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bonds:
\[\mathrm{CCl_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4Cl(g)}, \quad \Delta_a H^\circ = 4 \times \Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H\]

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
1. Enthalpy of formation of gaseous \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\):
\[\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(g)}] = \Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(l)}] + \Delta_{\text{vap}}H^\circ = -135.5 + 30.5 = -105.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
2. Reaction of formation of gaseous \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\):
\[\mathrm{C(s) + 2Cl_2(g) \rightarrow CCl_4(g)}\]
3. In terms of atomisation enthalpies and bond formation:
\[\Delta_f H^\circ[\mathrm{CCl_4(g)}] = \Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{C(s)}] + 2\,\Delta_a H^\circ[\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}] - 4\,\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute the values:
\[-105.0 = 715.0 + 2(242.0) - 4\,\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H\]
\[-105.0 = 715.0 + 484.0 - 4\,\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H\]
\[-105.0 = 1199.0 - 4\,\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H\]
Rearranging for the atomisation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{CCl_4(g)}\):
\[4\,\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H = 1199.0 + 105.0 = 1304.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
Calculate the mean bond enthalpy:
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{C-Cl}}H = \frac{1304.0}{4} = 326.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Bond enthalpies are positive quantities representing the energy required to homolytically break one mole of bonds.
The mean \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond enthalpy is \(326.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q19 - Temperature limit for process spontaneity

questiontext.text: For a given reaction, \(\Delta H = 400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = 0.2\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Above what temperature will the reaction become spontaneous, assuming \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) are constant over the temperature range?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Enthalpy change, \(\Delta H = 400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Entropy change, \(\Delta S = 0.2\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
For spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure, the Gibbs energy change must be negative: \(\Delta G < 0\).

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Gibbs-Helmholtz equation:
\[\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\]
At equilibrium, \(\Delta G = 0\), which gives the transition temperature:
\[T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Since both \(\Delta H > 0\) and \(\Delta S > 0\), the term \(-T\Delta S\) becomes more negative as temperature increases.
Setting \(\Delta G < 0\):
\[\Delta H - T\Delta S < 0 \implies T\Delta S > \Delta H \implies T > \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\]
Substitute the given values:
\[T > \frac{400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}{0.2\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}} = 2000\text{ K}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
At temperatures higher than \(2000\text{ K}\), \(T\Delta S\) exceeds \(\Delta H\), making \(\Delta G\) negative and the reaction spontaneous.
The reaction becomes spontaneous at \(T > 2000\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_NUMERICAL_Q20 - Standard Gibbs energy change from equilibrium constant

questiontext.text: The equilibrium constant for a reaction is \(10.0\) at \(300\text{ K}\). What is the value of \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)? (Take \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(\ln 10 \approx 2.303\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Given Data and Conditions:
Equilibrium constant, \(K = 10.0\).
Temperature, \(T = 300\text{ K}\).
Gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\ln 10 = 2.303\).

Step 2
Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Standard conditions apply for the relationship between the thermodynamic equilibrium constant and standard Gibbs energy.

Step 3
Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The relationship between standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant is:
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303\,RT\log_{10} K\]

Step 4
Step-by-Step Working:
Substitute the given values:
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2.303 \times (8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}) \times (300\text{ K}) \times \log_{10}(10.0)\]
Since \(\log_{10}(10.0) = 1\):
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 = -5744.14\text{ J mol}^{-1}\]
Convert to kilojoules:
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = \frac{-5744.14}{1000} \approx -5.74\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5
Check and Final Answer:
Since \(K > 1\), the reaction is exergonic under standard conditions, so \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) must be negative.
The value of \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) is \(-5.74\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q01 - Steps to measure heat of combustion

questiontext.text:
In a bomb calorimeter experiment designed to measure the internal energy change (\(\Delta U\)) during the combustion of an organic compound, the following operational steps are executed:

  1. A known mass of the combustible sample is placed in a platinum cup and sealed inside a rigid steel bomb pressurized with excess dioxygen.
  2. The sealed bomb is submerged in a known mass of water inside an insulated outer bucket equipped with a precision thermometer and a mechanical stirrer.
  3. The sample is ignited electrically using an ignition wire to initiate rapid and complete combustion inside the sealed bomb.
  4. The water bath is continuously stirred, the maximum temperature rise (\(\Delta T\)) is recorded, and the heat evolved at constant volume (\(q_V\)) is calculated using the calorimeter heat capacity.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of these operational steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Constant Volume Calorimetry
In bomb calorimetry, the volume of the reaction vessel remains constant (\(\Delta V = 0\)), ensuring that no expansion work is done (\(w = 0\)). Consequently, according to the First Law of Thermodynamics, the heat exchanged equals the internal energy change of the combustion reaction (\(q_V = \Delta U\)).

Step 2: Sample Preparation and Containment
The experiment begins by accurately weighing the combustible substance into a sample cup and sealing it inside a heavy steel vessel (the bomb) pressurized with excess oxygen gas (typically 20–30 atm) to guarantee complete combustion. Thus, sealing the combustible sample in the pressurized bomb is the initial step (I).

Step 3: Assembly of the Calorimetric Bath
Next, the sealed bomb is placed into the calorimeter bucket containing a predetermined mass of water. The bucket is placed inside an insulated water jacket to prevent heat exchange with the laboratory environment, and the stirrer and thermometer are installed. This corresponds to the second step (II).

Step 4: Combustion Initiation
Once thermal equilibrium is established between the bomb and the water bath, an electric current is passed through the ignition wire to combust the sample completely. This represents the third step (III).

Step 5: Temperature Monitoring and Thermal Evaluation
The heat liberated by the combustion reaction is transferred through the conductive steel walls to the stirred water bath. Stirring ensures uniform temperature distribution. The observer monitors the temperature rise until it reaches a maximum plateau (\(\Delta T\)), from which the heat evolved at constant volume is computed as \(q_V = C_V \Delta T\). This constitutes the final step (IV).

Therefore, the correct chronological sequence of operations is I → II → III → IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q02 - Sequence of cooling steam to ice

questiontext.text:
A 1.0 mol sample of superheated steam initially at \(120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{atm}\) is continuously cooled under constant pressure until it forms subcooled ice at \(-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Consider the following thermal and phase transition stages:

  1. Cooling of gaseous water vapor from \(120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to its condensation point at \(100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
  2. Condensation of water vapor into liquid water at a constant temperature of \(100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
  3. Cooling of liquid water from \(100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to its freezing point at \(0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
  4. Freezing of liquid water into solid ice at a constant temperature of \(0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
  5. Cooling of solid ice from \(0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) down to \(-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these thermal processes as heat is progressively removed from the system?

generalfeedback.text:
