Pairing each physical process with its defining equilibrium property establishes that liquid-vapour corresponds to constant vapour pressure, solid-liquid corresponds to fixed melting point, solid solute in solution corresponds to constant solute concentration, and gas dissolution corresponds to a constant concentration-to-pressure ratio.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q02 - Definitions of acid and base concepts

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Theory / Concept) List II (Fundamental Definition)
(A) Arrhenius acid (I) Species capable of accepting a proton \(\mathrm{(H^+)}\)
(B) Brönsted-Lowry base (II) Acid-base pair that differs by only one proton
(C) Lewis acid (III) Substance that dissociates in water to yield hydrogen ions \(\mathrm{H^+(aq)}\)
(D) Conjugate acid-base pair (IV) Electron pair acceptor species lacking an electron octet or having vacant orbitals

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Acid-Base Theories
Acid-base theories classify chemical species according to specific behavioral criteria: hydrogen/hydroxyl ion generation in aqueous solution (Arrhenius), proton transfer dynamics (Brönsted-Lowry), and electron pair exchange (Lewis).

Step 2: Evaluation of Respective Definitions
An Arrhenius acid is explicitly defined as a substance that dissociates in aqueous solution to yield hydrogen ions, \(\mathrm{H^+(aq)}\).
A Brönsted-Lowry base is defined as a proton acceptor, a species capable of gaining a hydrogen ion, \(\mathrm{H^+}\).
A Lewis acid is defined as an electron pair acceptor, which includes electron-deficient molecules like boron trifluoride or simple cations.
A conjugate acid-base pair consists of two species that interconvert through the transfer of a single proton, thus differing in formula by exactly one proton.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each theory to its fundamental principle associates the Arrhenius acid with water dissociation yielding hydrogen ions, the Brönsted-Lowry base with proton acceptance, the Lewis acid with electron pair acceptance, and the conjugate pair with species differing by a single proton.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q03 - Identification of conjugate acid base pairs

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Reacting Species Behavior) List II (Conjugate Species Formed)
(A) \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\) acting as a Brönsted acid (I) \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) acting as a Brönsted base (II) \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) acting as a Brönsted base (III) \(\mathrm{OH^-}\)
(D) \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) acting as a Brönsted acid (IV) \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Conjugate Pairs
According to the Brönsted-Lowry concept, when a species donates a proton \(\mathrm{(H^+)}\), it acts as an acid and generates its conjugate base, which possesses one less proton. Conversely, when a species accepts a proton, it acts as a base and generates its conjugate acid, which possesses one extra proton.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Proton Transfer Reactions
When hydrogencarbonate ion, \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\), behaves as an acid, it releases a proton: \[\mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightarrow H^+ + CO_3^{2-}}\] The resulting conjugate base formed is carbonate ion, \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\).
When ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), behaves as a base, it gains a proton: \[\mathrm{NH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow NH_4^+}\] The resulting conjugate acid formed is ammonium ion, \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\).
When hydrogen sulphate ion, \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\), behaves as a base, it gains a proton: \[\mathrm{HSO_4^- + H^+ \rightarrow H_2SO_4}\] The resulting conjugate acid formed is sulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).
When water, \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), acts as an acid, it donates a proton: \[\mathrm{H_2O \rightarrow H^+ + OH^-}\] The resulting conjugate base formed is hydroxide ion, \(\mathrm{OH^-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Connecting the acting species to their corresponding conjugate products establishes hydrogencarbonate as an acid yielding carbonate, ammonia as a base yielding ammonium, hydrogen sulphate as a base yielding sulphuric acid, and water as an acid yielding hydroxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q04 - Reaction quotient and equilibrium thermodynamic criteria

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Thermodynamic / Kinetic Condition) List II (System State / Reaction Feature)
(A) \(Q_c < K_c\) (I) Net reaction proceeds spontaneously in the forward direction towards products
(B) \(K_c > 10^3\) (II) System has reached dynamic chemical equilibrium with no net driving force
(C) \(\Delta G^{\circ} < 0\) (III) Products predominate overwhelmingly and reaction proceeds nearly to completion
(D) \(\Delta G = 0\) (IV) Equilibrium constant \(K > 1\), with forward reaction favored in the standard state

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Equilibrium Thermodynamics and Reaction Direction
The progress, extent, and spontaneity of chemical reactions are dictated by the relation between the reaction quotient \(Q_c\) and equilibrium constant \(K_c\), the magnitude of \(K_c\), and the Gibbs free energy functions \(\Delta G\) and \(\Delta G^{\circ}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
When the reaction quotient is less than the equilibrium constant, \(Q_c < K_c\), the ratio of products to reactants is lower than the equilibrium ratio; hence, reactants continue to react to form more products, driving a net forward reaction.
When the equilibrium constant is very large, \(K_c > 10^3\), the equilibrium concentrations of products greatly exceed those of reactants, meaning the reaction proceeds almost to completion.
According to \(\Delta G^{\circ} = -RT \ln K\), a negative standard Gibbs energy, \(\Delta G^{\circ} < 0\), implies that \(\ln K > 0\), meaning \(K > 1\) and standard state thermodynamics favour product formation.
When the real-time Gibbs free energy change reaches zero, \(\Delta G = 0\), the forward and backward process rates balance each other, signifying the attainment of dynamic equilibrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Correlating each thermodynamic condition with its physical outcome links \(Q_c < K_c\) with forward net reaction, \(K_c > 10^3\) with near completion, \(\Delta G^{\circ} < 0\) with \(K > 1\), and \(\Delta G = 0\) with dynamic equilibrium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q05 - Le Chatelier principle response to stresses

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Perturbation Applied to System) List II (Directional Response of Equilibrium)
(A) Increasing total pressure on \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\) (I) Equilibrium remains completely undisturbed with no change in composition
(B) Decreasing temperature of \(2\mathrm{NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)}\) (\(\Delta H < 0\)) (II) Shifts forward favoring exothermic formation of the colourless dimer
(C) Adding argon gas at constant volume to \(\mathrm{CO(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_4(g) + H_2O(g)}\) (III) Continually drives thermal dissociation forward toward completion
(D) Continuous removal of \(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\) from \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}\) (IV) Shifts forward toward the side with fewer moles of gaseous species

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Principle
Le Chatelier's principle dictates that when an external constraint (temperature, pressure, volume, or concentration) is imposed on a system at dynamic equilibrium, the system adjusts in such a direction as to counteract the applied stress.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Analysis of Perturbations
In the synthesis of ammonia, \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\), the reactant side has \(4\text{ moles}\) of gas while the product side has \(2\text{ moles}\). Increasing pressure forces the system to reduce pressure by shifting forward toward fewer gaseous moles.
In the dimerisation reaction \(2\mathrm{NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)}\), the forward formation of dinitrogen tetroxide is exothermic (\(\Delta H = -57.2\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)). Lowering the temperature causes the system to release heat by shifting in the forward direction, favoring the formation of the dimer.
Adding an inert gas such as argon at constant volume does not alter the partial pressures or molar concentrations of the reacting gases, meaning the reaction quotient remains identical to the equilibrium constant and the equilibrium is unaffected.
Continuously removing the gaseous product, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), keeps its partial pressure below the equilibrium value, maintaining \(Q_p < K_p\) and driving the decomposition of calcium carbonate forward to completion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Correlating each disturbance to its equilibrium behavior pairs pressure increase in ammonia synthesis with shifting to fewer gas moles, temperature decrease in nitrogen dioxide dimerisation with forward exothermic shift, argon addition at constant volume with no disturbance, and continuous carbon dioxide removal with forward drive to completion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q06 - Hydrolysis characteristics of different salt types

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Salt Formula) List II (Hydrolysis Nature and Solution pH)
(A) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) (I) Cationic hydrolysis produces excess hydronium ions, yielding an acidic solution with \(\mathrm{pH} < 7\)
(B) \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\) (II) Neither cation nor anion hydrolyses, giving a neutral aqueous solution with \(\mathrm{pH} = 7\)
(C) \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) (III) Both ions hydrolyse, with \(\mathrm{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_b) \approx 7.005\)
(D) \(\mathrm{CH_3COONH_4}\) (\(\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.76, \mathrm{p}K_b = 4.75\)) (IV) Anionic hydrolysis produces excess hydroxyl ions, yielding a basic solution with \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Salt Hydrolysis
Salt hydrolysis involves the interaction of salt cations, anions, or both with water. Cations of strong bases and anions of strong acids do not hydrolyse; they simply undergo hydration. Salts derived from weak components undergo hydrolysis, altering the hydrogen and hydroxide ion balance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Specific Salt
Sodium chloride, \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), is formed from a strong acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) and a strong base (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)). Neither \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) nor \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) hydrolyses; hence, the solution remains neutral with \(\mathrm{pH} = 7\).
Sodium acetate, \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\), is formed from a weak acid and a strong base. The acetate anion undergoes hydrolysis: \[\mathrm{CH_3COO^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_3COOH + OH^-}\] This generates excess \(\mathrm{OH^-}\), resulting in an alkaline solution with \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\).
Ammonium chloride, \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\), is formed from a strong acid and a weak base. The ammonium cation undergoes hydrolysis: \[\mathrm{NH_4^+ + H_2O \rightleftharpoons NH_4OH + H^+}\] This generates excess \(\mathrm{H^+}\), producing an acidic solution with \(\mathrm{pH} < 7\).
Ammonium acetate, \(\mathrm{CH_3COONH_4}\), is formed from a weak acid and a weak base. Both ions hydrolyse, and the resulting pH is given by: \[\mathrm{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_b) = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(4.76 - 4.75) = 7.005\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each salt to its aqueous solution characteristic pairs sodium chloride with neutral non-hydrolysing behavior, sodium acetate with anionic hydrolysis and basic pH, ammonium chloride with cationic hydrolysis and acidic pH, and ammonium acetate with dual hydrolysis yielding pH near 7.005.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q07 - Solubility product expressions for ionic salts

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II (where \(S\) represents the molar solubility of each sparingly soluble salt in pure water in \(\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}\)):

List I (Sparingly Soluble Salt) List II (Solubility Product Constant \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\))
(A) \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) (I) \(4S^3\)
(B) \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\) (II) \(6912S^7\)
(C) \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) (III) \(S^2\)
(D) \(\mathrm{Zr_3(PO_4)_4}\) (IV) \(27S^4\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle and Formula
For a sparingly soluble salt of stoichiometry \(\mathrm{M}_x\mathrm{X}_y\) dissociating according to: \[\mathrm{M}_x\mathrm{X}_y\mathrm{(s)} \rightleftharpoons x\,\mathrm{M}^{p+}\mathrm{(aq)} + y\,\mathrm{X}^{q-}\mathrm{(aq)}\] where molar solubility is \(S\), the ionic concentrations are \([\mathrm{M}^{p+}] = xS\) and \([\mathrm{X}^{q-}] = yS\). The solubility product constant is: \[K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [\mathrm{M}^{p+}]^x [\mathrm{X}^{q-}]^y = (xS)^x (yS)^y = x^x \cdot y^y \cdot S^{(x+y)}\]

Step 2: Step-by-Step Derivations
For barium sulphate, \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\): \[\mathrm{BaSO_4(s) \rightleftharpoons Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\] Here \(x = 1, y = 1\), giving: \[K_{\mathrm{sp}} = (S)(S) = S^2\]
For calcium fluoride, \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\): \[\mathrm{CaF_2(s) \rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}(aq) + 2F^-(aq)}\] Here \(x = 1, y = 2\), giving: \[K_{\mathrm{sp}} = (S)(2S)^2 = 4S^3\]
For aluminium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\): \[\mathrm{Al(OH)_3(s) \rightleftharpoons Al^{3+}(aq) + 3OH^-(aq)}\] Here \(x = 1, y = 3\), giving: \[K_{\mathrm{sp}} = (S)(3S)^3 = 27S^4\]
For zirconium phosphate, \(\mathrm{Zr_3(PO_4)_4}\): \[\mathrm{Zr_3(PO_4)_4(s) \rightleftharpoons 3Zr^{4+}(aq) + 4PO_4^{3-}(aq)}\] Here \(x = 3, y = 4\), giving: \[K_{\mathrm{sp}} = (3S)^3 (4S)^4 = 27 \times 256 \times S^7 = 6912S^7\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each salt with its algebraic relationship yields barium sulphate matching \(S^2\), calcium fluoride matching \(4S^3\), aluminium hydroxide matching \(27S^4\), and zirconium phosphate matching \(6912S^7\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q08 - Calculations of pH for various solutions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II (all values measured at \(298\text{ K}\)):

List I (Aqueous System) List II (Resulting \(\mathrm{pH}\))
(A) \(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}\) aqueous \(\mathrm{HCl}\) solution (I) \(4.74\)
(B) Buffer containing \(0.05\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) and \(0.05\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\) (\(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\)) (II) \(6.98\)
(C) Buffer containing equimolar \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) (\(\mathrm{p}K_b = 4.75\)) (IV) \(9.25\)
(D) \(0.08\text{ M}\) aqueous \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) solution (\(K_a = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\)) (III) \(2.85\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions and Formulae
The pH of aqueous systems is evaluated using: \[\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\] where contributions from water autodissociation must be accounted for in very dilute strong acids, Henderson-Hasselbalch relations apply to buffers, and Ostwald dilution logic applies to weak acids.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculations line by line
For \(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}\) hydrochloric acid, hydronium ions originate both from \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and from water autoionization: \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 10^{-8} + x\), where \([\mathrm{OH^-}] = x\). Setting \(K_w = (10^{-8} + x)x = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\) yields: \[x^2 + 10^{-8}x - 10^{-14} = 0\] Solving the quadratic equation gives \(x = 9.5 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}\). Thus, \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} + 9.5 \times 10^{-8} = 1.05 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}\), giving \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(1.05 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.98\).
For the acidic buffer with equimolar \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}\), \([\text{Salt}] = [\text{Acid}] = 0.05\text{ M}\). According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: \[\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} = -\log(1.8 \times 10^{-5}) + \log(1) = 4.74 + 0 = 4.74\]
For the basic buffer with equimolar \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\), \(\mathrm{pOH} = \mathrm{p}K_b + \log\frac{[\text{Conjugate acid}]}{[\text{Base}]} = 4.75 + 0 = 4.75\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{pH} = 14 - \mathrm{pOH} = 14 - 4.75 = 9.25\).
For \(0.08\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), the ionization equilibrium is \(\mathrm{HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^-}\). With \(x \ll 0.08\): \[K_a = \frac{x^2}{0.08} = 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \implies x^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \implies x = [\mathrm{H^+}] = 1.41 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\] The resulting pH is \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(1.41 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.85\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each solution with its determined pH assigns the dilute hydrochloric acid solution to \(6.98\), the acetic acid buffer to \(4.74\), the ammonia buffer to \(9.25\), and the hypochlorous acid solution to \(2.85\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q09 - Relation between equilibrium constants Kp Kc

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Gaseous Equilibrium Reaction) List II (Mathematical Relation between \(K_p\) and \(K_c\))
(A) \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\) (I) \(K_p = K_c(RT)\)
(B) \(2\mathrm{NOCl(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g) + Cl_2(g)}\) (II) \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\) (III) \(K_p = K_c\)
(D) \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + H_2O(g) \rightleftharpoons CO(g) + 3H_2(g)}\) (IV) \(K_p = K_c(RT)^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Relationship
For a general reversible gaseous reaction, the pressure-based equilibrium constant \(K_p\) and concentration-based equilibrium constant \(K_c\) are interconnected by the relation: \[K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}\] where \(\Delta n\) is the change in the number of gaseous moles, defined as: \[\Delta n = (\text{moles of gaseous products}) - (\text{moles of gaseous reactants})\]

Step 2: Step-by-Step Evaluation of Stoichiometric Differences
For the formation of hydrogen iodide, \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\): \[\Delta n = 2 - (1 + 1) = 0 \implies K_p = K_c(RT)^0 = K_c\]
For the decomposition of nitrosyl chloride, \(2\mathrm{NOCl(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g) + Cl_2(g)}\): \[\Delta n = (2 + 1) - 2 = 3 - 2 = 1 \implies K_p = K_c(RT)^1 = K_c(RT)\]
For the Haber synthesis of ammonia, \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\): \[\Delta n = 2 - (1 + 3) = 2 - 4 = -2 \implies K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}\]
For the methane steam reforming reaction, \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + H_2O(g) \rightleftharpoons CO(g) + 3H_2(g)}\): \[\Delta n = (1 + 3) - (1 + 1) = 4 - 2 = 2 \implies K_p = K_c(RT)^2\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each gaseous reaction with its corresponding equation yields hydrogen iodide synthesis with \(K_p = K_c\), nitrosyl chloride decomposition with \(K_p = K_c(RT)\), ammonia formation with \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}\), and steam-methane reforming with \(K_p = K_c(RT)^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCHING_Q10 - Chemical equation manipulation and equilibrium constants

questiontext.text:
Given the reference reaction for the synthesis of ammonia:

\[\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)} \quad \text{with equilibrium constant } K_c\]

Match List I with List II:

List I (Modified Chemical Equation) List II (Resulting Equilibrium Constant)
(A) \(2\mathrm{NH_3(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2(g) + 3H_2(g)}\) (I) \((K_c)^{1/2}\)
(B) \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \frac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3(g)}\) (II) \((K_c)^2\)
(C) \(\mathrm{NH_3(g)} \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \frac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) (III) \(\frac{1}{K_c}\)
(D) \(2\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 4\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\) (IV) \((K_c)^{-1/2}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Rules for Equilibrium Constant Transformation
From the law of chemical equilibrium, altering the stoichiometric form of an equation changes the mathematical expression for the equilibrium constant:
1. Reversing a chemical equation replaces the equilibrium constant with its reciprocal: \(K' = \frac{1}{K}\).
2. Multiplying all stoichiometric coefficients by a factor \(n\) raises the equilibrium constant to the power \(n\): \(K'' = K^n\).
3. Simultaneously reversing an equation and multiplying by \(n\) gives \(K''' = (K)^{-n}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Application to Each Transformation
The equation \(2\mathrm{NH_3(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2(g) + 3H_2(g)}\) is obtained by reversing the reference equation without changing stoichiometric numbers; hence, its equilibrium constant is \(\frac{1}{K_c}\).
The equation \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \frac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3(g)}\) is obtained by multiplying the forward reference reaction by \(\frac{1}{2}\); hence, its equilibrium constant is \((K_c)^{1/2}\).
The equation \(\mathrm{NH_3(g)} \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \frac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) is obtained by reversing the reference reaction and multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2}\); hence, its equilibrium constant is \((K_c)^{-1/2}\).
The equation \(2\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 4\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\) is obtained by multiplying the forward reference reaction by \(2\); hence, its equilibrium constant is \((K_c)^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each modified equation to its resulting equilibrium constant links the simple reverse reaction with \(\frac{1}{K_c}\), the halved forward reaction with \((K_c)^{1/2}\), the halved reverse reaction with \((K_c)^{-1/2}\), and the doubled forward reaction with \((K_c)^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q01 - Equilibrium constant for nitric oxide synthesis

questiontext.text:
At 800 K, a reaction mixture at equilibrium in a closed vessel contains \( [\mathrm{N}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \), \( [\mathrm{O}_2] = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \), and \( [\mathrm{NO}] = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \) for the reaction:
\[ \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) \]
What is the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the reaction at this temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Equilibrium concentration of nitrogen gas: \( [\mathrm{N}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Equilibrium concentration of oxygen gas: \( [\mathrm{O}_2] = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Equilibrium concentration of nitric oxide gas: \( [\mathrm{NO}] = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Temperature of the closed system: \( T = 800\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The reaction takes place in a closed vessel at constant temperature and has reached dynamic chemical equilibrium. The gases behave ideally, so molar concentrations are directly applicable in the equilibrium law expression.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For the balanced chemical equation \( \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) \), the equilibrium constant expression in terms of molar concentrations is:
\[ K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{NO}]^2}{[\mathrm{N}_2][\mathrm{O}_2]} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the expression:
\[ K_c = \frac{(2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M})^2}{(3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M})(4.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M})} \]
Evaluate the numerator:
\[ (2.8 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 7.84 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{M}^2 \]
Evaluate the denominator:
\[ (3.0 \times 10^{-3}) \times (4.2 \times 10^{-3}) = 1.26 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}^2 \]
Divide the numerator by the denominator:
\[ K_c = \frac{7.84 \times 10^{-6}}{1.26 \times 10^{-5}} = \frac{7.84}{12.6} \approx 0.622 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the change in moles of gas is \( \Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 1) = 0 \), the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) is dimensionless. The arithmetic confirms that \( K_c \approx 0.622 \).
Final Answer: \( 0.622 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q02 - Equilibrium constant for phosphorus pentachloride decomposition

questiontext.text:
A 10.0 L vessel contains 0.15 mol of \( \mathrm{PCl}_5 \), 0.20 mol of \( \mathrm{PCl}_3 \), and 0.20 mol of \( \mathrm{Cl}_2 \) at equilibrium at 500 K according to the reaction:
\[ \mathrm{PCl}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_3(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g}) \]
What is the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the reaction at 500 K?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Volume of reaction vessel: \( V = 10.0\ \text{L} \).
Equilibrium amount of \( \mathrm{PCl}_5 \): \( n_{\mathrm{PCl}_5} = 0.15\ \text{mol} \).
Equilibrium amount of \( \mathrm{PCl}_3 \): \( n_{\mathrm{PCl}_3} = 0.20\ \text{mol} \).
Equilibrium amount of \( \mathrm{Cl}_2 \): \( n_{\mathrm{Cl}_2} = 0.20\ \text{mol} \).
Temperature: \( T = 500\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Molar concentration equals the number of moles divided by the total volume in liters: \( c = \frac{n}{V} \). The gases are assumed to be in homogenous chemical equilibrium.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant expression for the dissociation reaction is:
\[ K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{PCl}_3][\mathrm{Cl}_2]}{[\mathrm{PCl}_5]} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate molar concentrations of each species:
\[ [\mathrm{PCl}_5] = \frac{0.15\ \text{mol}}{10.0\ \text{L}} = 0.015\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \]
\[ [\mathrm{PCl}_3] = \frac{0.20\ \text{mol}}{10.0\ \text{L}} = 0.020\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \]
\[ [\mathrm{Cl}_2] = \frac{0.20\ \text{mol}}{10.0\ \text{L}} = 0.020\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \]
Substitute the concentrations into the expression for \( K_c \):
\[ K_c = \frac{(0.020)(0.020)}{0.015} = \frac{0.00040}{0.015} = \frac{4}{150} \approx 0.0267\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} = 2.67 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \]
Final Answer: \( 2.67 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The reaction has \( \Delta n_g = (1 + 1) - 1 = 1 \), yielding units of \( \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \) (or \( \text{M} \)). The calculated value \( 2.67 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \) matches the stoichiometry.
Final Answer: \( 2.67 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q03 - Calculation of pH of soft drink sample

questiontext.text: The hydrogen ion concentration in a sample of a soft drink is measured to be \( 3.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \). What is the pH of this soft drink? (Given: \( \log_{10}(3.8) \approx 0.58 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Hydrogen ion concentration: \( [\mathrm{H}^+] = 3.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \).
Logarithmic value given: \( \log_{10}(3.8) = 0.58 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The pH of an aqueous solution is defined as the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion activity, approximated by molar concentration in dilute solution.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ \text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\\mathrm{H}^+] \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the hydrogen ion concentration into the formula:
\[ \text{pH} = -\log_{10}(3.8 \times 10^{-3}) \]
Using logarithmic properties \( \log_{10}(a \times 10^{-b}) = \log_{10}(a) - b \):
\[ \text{pH} = -(\log_{10}(3.8) + \log_{10}(10^{-3})) \]
\[ \text{pH} = -(0.58 - 3) = 3 - 0.58 = 2.42 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the solution is acidic with \( [\mathrm{H}^+] > 10^{-7}\ \text{M} \), the pH must be below 7. With \( [\mathrm{H}^+] \) between \( 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \) and \( 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \), the pH must lie between 2 and 3, precisely matching 2.42.
Final Answer: \( 2.42 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q04 - Equilibrium constant for calcium carbonate thermal decomposition

questiontext.text:
In a closed vessel at 1073 K, calcium carbonate decomposes according to the heterogeneous equilibrium:
\[ \mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \]
If the equilibrium partial pressure of \( \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \) is 0.40 atm, what is the value of \( K_p \) for this decomposition reaction at 1073 K?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \( \mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \).
Temperature: \( T = 1073\ \text{K} \).
Equilibrium partial pressure of carbon dioxide: \( p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 0.40\ \text{atm} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Pure solids have constant molar concentrations, so their activities are taken as unity (1) in the equilibrium constant expression.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant expression in terms of partial pressures is given by:
\[ K_p = p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because both \( \mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \) and \( \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) \) are pure solids, they do not appear in the expression for \( K_p \):
\[ K_p = p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 0.40\ \text{atm} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The value of \( K_p \) depends solely on the partial pressure of gaseous carbon dioxide in equilibrium with the solid phases at constant temperature. Hence, \( K_p = 0.40\ \text{atm} \).
Final Answer: \( 0.40\ \text{atm} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q05 - Equilibrium constant for Haber ammonia synthesis

questiontext.text:
For the synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gases:
\[ \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g}) \]
The concentrations of species at equilibrium at 500 K are found to be \( [\mathrm{N}_2] = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \), \( [\mathrm{H}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \), and \( [\mathrm{NH}_3] = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M} \).
What is the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Equilibrium concentration of \( \mathrm{N}_2 \): \( [\mathrm{N}_2] = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Equilibrium concentration of \( \mathrm{H}_2 \): \( [\mathrm{H}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Equilibrium concentration of \( \mathrm{NH}_3 \): \( [\mathrm{NH}_3] = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Temperature: \( T = 500\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The system is at thermodynamic equilibrium in a closed vessel, and stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation serve as powers of concentration terms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By the Law of Mass Action:
\[ K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{NH}_3]^2}{[\mathrm{N}_2][\mathrm{H}_2]^3} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given concentrations into the expression:
\[ K_c = \frac{(1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M})^2}{(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M})(3.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{M})^3} \]
Compute the numerator:
\[ (1.2 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 1.44 \times 10^{-4} \]
Compute each factor in the denominator:
\[ (3.0 \times 10^{-2})^3 = 2.7 \times 10^{-5} \]
\[ [\mathrm{N}_2][\mathrm{H}_2]^3 = (1.5 \times 10^{-2}) \times (2.7 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.05 \times 10^{-7} \]
Calculate \( K_c \):
\[ K_c = \frac{1.44 \times 10^{-4}}{4.05 \times 10^{-7}} = \frac{1.44}{4.05} \times 10^3 \approx 0.3556 \times 10^3 = 3.56 \times 10^2\ \text{M}^{-2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units are \( \text{M}^{2 - (1 + 3)} = \text{M}^{-2} \). The magnitude is consistent with significant figures from the input concentrations.
Final Answer: \( 3.56 \times 10^2\ \text{M}^{-2} \\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q06 - Equilibrium constant for sulfur trioxide formation

questiontext.text:
In a 2.0 L closed reaction vessel at 450 K, equilibrium is reached for the reaction:
\[ 2\mathrm{SO}_2(\\mathrm{g}) + \\mathrm{O}_2(\\mathrm{g}) \\rightleftharpoons 2\\mathrm{SO}_3(\\mathrm{g}) \]
The equilibrium amounts of the components are found to be 0.60 mol of \( \mathrm{SO}_2 \), 0.82 mol of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \), and 1.90 mol of \( \mathrm{SO}_3 \).
What is the numerical value of \( K_c \) for the reaction at this temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Volume of vessel: \( V = 2.0\ \text{L} \).
Equilibrium moles of \( \mathrm{SO}_2 \): \( n_{\mathrm{SO}_2} = 0.60\ \text{mol} \).
Equilibrium moles of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \): \( n_{\mathrm{O}_2} = 0.82\ \text{mol} \).
Equilibrium moles of \( \mathrm{SO}_3 \): \( n_{\mathrm{SO}_3} = 1.90\ \text{mol} \).
Temperature: \( T = 450\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Concentrations are obtained by dividing moles by the total volume of 2.0 L before setting up the equilibrium constant expression.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant expression is:
\[ K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{SO}_3]^2}{[\mathrm{SO}_2]^2 [\mathrm{O}_2]} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Determine the equilibrium molar concentrations:
\[ [\mathrm{SO}_2] = \frac{0.60\ \text{mol}}{2.0\ \text{L}} = 0.30\ \text{M} \]
\[ [\mathrm{O}_2] = \frac{0.82\ \text{mol}}{2.0\ \text{L}} = 0.41\ \text{M} \]
\[ [\mathrm{SO}_3] = \frac{1.90\ \text{mol}}{2.0\ \text{L}} = 0.95\ \text{M} \]
Substitute into the \( K_c \) formula:
\[ K_c = \frac{(0.95)^2}{(0.30)^2 \times (0.41)} \]
Calculate numerator and denominator:
\[ (0.95)^2 = 0.9025 \]
\[ (0.30)^2 \times 0.41 = 0.09 \times 0.41 = 0.0369 \]
\[ K_c = \frac{0.9025}{0.0369} \approx 24.458 \approx 24.46\ \text{M}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \( \text{M}^{2 - (2 + 1)} = \text{M}^{-1} \). Omitting the 2.0 L volume yields 12.23, confirming that accounting for vessel volume gives 24.46.
Final Answer: \( 24.46\ \text{M}^{-1} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q07 - Conversion between equilibrium constants Kp and Kc

questiontext.text:
At 1069 K, the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the thermal decomposition of nitrosyl chloride:
\[ 2\mathrm{NOCl}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g}) \]
is \( 3.75 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \). What is the value of \( K_p \) for this reaction at 1069 K?
(Take \( R = 0.0831\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Equilibrium constant in concentration terms: \( K_c = 3.75 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
Temperature: \( T = 1069\ \text{K} \).
Universal gas constant: \( R = 0.0831\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
All species in the reaction mixture behave as ideal gases, so the relation connecting \( K_p \) and \( K_c \) holds precisely.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g} \]
where \( \Delta n_g = \sum n_{\text{gaseous products}} - \sum n_{\text{gaseous reactants}} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Determine \( \Delta n_g \) for the balanced reaction \( 2\mathrm{NOCl}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g}) \):
\[ \Delta n_g = (2 + 1) - 2 = 3 - 2 = 1 \]
Calculate the product \( RT \):
\[ RT = 0.0831\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \times 1069\ \text{K} = 88.8339\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \]
Compute \( K_p \):
\[ K_p = K_c(RT)^1 = (3.75 \times 10^{-6}) \times 88.8339 \]
\[ K_p = 333.13 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{bar} = 3.33 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{bar} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
With \( \Delta n_g = +1 \), \( K_p > K_c \) in numerical magnitude when \( RT > 1 \). Since \( RT \approx 88.8 \), multiplying \( 3.75 \times 10^{-6} \) by 88.8 gives \( 3.33 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{bar} \).
Final Answer: \( 3.33 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{bar} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q08 - Standard Gibbs energy change of sucrose hydrolysis

questiontext.text:
The equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the hydrolysis of sucrose:
\[ \text{Sucrose} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{Glucose} + \text{Fructose} \]
is \( 2.0 \times 10^{13} \) at 300 K. What is the standard Gibbs free energy change \( \Delta G^\circ \) for the reaction at this temperature?
(Take \( R = 8.314\ \text{J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \) and \( \ln(2.0 \times 10^{13}) \approx 30.63 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Equilibrium constant: \( K_c = 2.0 \times 10^{13} \).
Temperature: \( T = 300\ \text{K} \).
Gas constant: \( R = 8.314\ \text{J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \).
Natural logarithm value: \( \ln(2.0 \times 10^{13}) = 30.63 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The thermodynamic relationship connecting standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant applies under standard state conditions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ \Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values into the thermodynamic equation:
\[ \Delta G^\circ = -(8.314\ \text{J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}) \times (300\ \text{K}) \times (30.63) \]
Calculate the product of \( R \) and \( T \):
\[ RT = 8.314 \times 300 = 2494.2\ \text{J}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \]
Multiply by \( \ln K \):
\[ \Delta G^\circ = -2494.2 \times 30.63 = -76402.3\ \text{J}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \]
Convert joules to kilojoules:
\[ \Delta G^\circ = -\frac{76402.3}{1000}\ \text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \approx -76.4\ \text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \( K \gg 1 \), the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions, mandating a negative value for \( \Delta G^\circ \). The value \( -76.4\ \text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \) is thermodynamically consistent.
Final Answer: \( -76.4\ \text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q09 - Calculation of pH of pure water at elevated temperature

questiontext.text:
At 310 K (human body temperature), the ionic product of water \( K_w \) is \( 2.7 \times 10^{-14} \). What is the pH of pure neutral water at this temperature?
(Given: \( \log_{10}(2.7) \approx 0.431 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Ionic product of water: \( K_w = 2.7 \times 10^{-14} \) at \( T = 310\ \text{K} \).
Logarithm value: \( \log_{10}(2.7) = 0.431 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
In pure water, autoionization produces equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions:
\[ [\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+] = [\mathrm{OH}^-] \]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By definition of the autoionization of water:
\[ K_w = [\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+][\mathrm{OH}^-] = [\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+]^2 \]
Taking the negative logarithm on both sides:
\[ pK_w = -\log_{10} K_w \]
\[ \text{pH} = \frac{1}{2} pK_w \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( pK_w \):
\[ pK_w = -\log_{10}(2.7 \times 10^{-14}) = 14 - \log_{10}(2.7) = 14 - 0.431 = 13.569 \]
Calculate the pH of the neutral solution:
\[ \text{pH} = \frac{13.569}{2} \approx 6.7845 \approx 6.78 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because water autoionization is endothermic, increasing temperature increases \( K_w \), shifting neutral pH below 7.00. The calculated value of 6.78 is chemically valid and remains strictly neutral.
Final Answer: \( 6.78 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q10 - Dissociation constant of a weak monobasic acid

questiontext.text:
The pH of a 0.10 M solution of a weak organic monobasic acid is 4.50. What is the acid dissociation constant \( K_a \) of this acid?
(Given: \( 10^{-0.50} \approx 0.316 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial concentration of weak acid: \( c = 0.10\ \text{M} \).
Solution pH: \( \text{pH} = 4.50 \).
Antilogarithmic value: \( 10^{-0.50} = 0.316 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
For a weak monobasic acid \( \mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{A}^- \), ionization is very small (\( [\mathrm{H}^+] \ll c \)), so \( [\mathrm{HA}] \approx c \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ [\mathrm{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} \]
\[ K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+][\mathrm{A}^-]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} \approx \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+]^2}{c} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( [\mathrm{H}^+] \):
\[ [\mathrm{H}^+] = 10^{-4.50} = 10^{-0.50} \times 10^{-4} = 0.316 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M} = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \]
Square the hydrogen ion concentration:
\[ [\mathrm{H}^+]^2 = (3.16 \times 10^{-5})^2 = 1.00 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{M}^2 \]
Calculate \( K_a \):
\[ K_a = \frac{1.00 \times 10^{-9}}{0.10} = 1.00 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Degree of dissociation is \( \alpha = \frac{3.16 \times 10^{-5}}{0.10} = 3.16 \times 10^{-4} = 0.0316\% \ll 5\% \), fully validating the approximation \( c - [\mathrm{H}^+] \approx c \). The calculated value is \( 1.00 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M} \).
Final Answer: \( 1.00 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q11 - Percent ionization of hypochlorous acid solution

questiontext.text:
The ionization constant \( K_a \) of hypochlorous acid (\( \mathrm{HOCl} \)) is \( 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \) at 298 K. What is the percent dissociation of \( \mathrm{HOCl} \) in a 0.08 M aqueous solution?
(Given: \( \sqrt{3.125} \approx 1.77 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Ionization constant of hypochlorous acid: \( K_a = 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \).
Initial concentration: \( c = 0.08\ \text{M} \).
Square root value: \( \sqrt{3.125} = 1.77 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Assuming degree of dissociation \( \alpha < 0.05 \) (5%), the denominator \( 1 - \alpha \) can be approximated as unity in Ostwald's dilution law.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \approx c \alpha^2 \]
\[ \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{c}} \]
\[ \text{Percent dissociation} = \alpha \times 100\% \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( \alpha \):
\[ \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{2.5 \times 10^{-5}}{0.08}} = \sqrt{\frac{25 \times 10^{-6}}{8 \times 10^{-2}}} = \sqrt{3.125 \times 10^{-4}} \]
Extract the root:
\[ \alpha = 1.77 \times 10^{-2} = 0.0177 \]
Convert to percentage:
\[ \text{Percent dissociation} = 0.0177 \times 100\% = 1.77\% \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \( 1.77\% < 5\% \), the approximation \( 1 - \alpha \approx 1 \) is verified to be accurate. The percent dissociation is 1.77%.
Final Answer: \( 1.77\% \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q12 - Base dissociation constant and pKb of hydrazine

questiontext.text:
The pH of a 0.004 M aqueous solution of hydrazine (\( \mathrm{NH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2 \)) is measured to be 9.70 at 298 K. What is the value of \( pK_b \) for hydrazine?
(Given: \( 10^{-0.30} \approx 0.501 \) and \( \log_{10}(6.28) \approx 0.80 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial base concentration: \( c = 0.004\ \text{M} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M} \).
Solution pH: \( \text{pH} = 9.70 \).
Logarithmic values: \( 10^{-0.30} = 0.501 \), \( \log_{10}(6.28) = 0.80 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Hydrazine acts as a weak base: \( \mathrm{B} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{BH}^+ + \mathrm{OH}^- \). Water autoionization at 298 K satisfies \( \text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14.00 \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ \text{pOH} = 14.00 - \text{pH} \]
\[ [\mathrm{OH}^-] = 10^{-\text{pOH}} \]
\[ K_b \approx \frac{[\mathrm{OH}^-]^2}{c} \]
\[ pK_b = -\log_{10} K_b \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Find pOH:
\[ \text{pOH} = 14.00 - 9.70 = 4.30 \]
Find hydroxide ion concentration:
\[ [\mathrm{OH}^-] = 10^{-4.30} = 10^{-0.30} \times 10^{-4} = 0.501 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M} = 5.01 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \]
Calculate \( K_b \):
\[ K_b = \frac{(5.01 \times 10^{-5})^2}{0.004} = \frac{2.51 \times 10^{-9}}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 6.28 \times 10^{-7} \]
Calculate \( pK_b \):
\[ pK_b = -\log_{10}(6.28 \times 10^{-7}) = 7 - \log_{10}(6.28) = 7 - 0.80 = 6.20 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The calculation confirms that \( [\mathrm{OH}^-] = 5.01 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \ll 0.004\ \text{M} \), justifying the approximation. The resulting \( pK_b \) is 6.20.
Final Answer: \( 6.20 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q13 - Calculation of pH of ammonium acetate salt solution

questiontext.text: What is the pH of a 0.05 M aqueous solution of ammonium acetate (\( \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONH}_4 \)) at 298 K, given that \( pK_a \) of acetic acid is 4.76 and \( pK_b \) of ammonium hydroxide is 4.75?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration of ammonium acetate salt: \( c = 0.05\ \text{M} \).
\( pK_a \) of weak acid (acetic acid): \( pK_a = 4.76 \).
\( pK_b \) of weak base (ammonia): \( pK_b = 4.75 \).
Temperature: \( T = 298\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Ammonium acetate is a salt formed from a weak acid and a weak base. Its hydrolysis pH is independent of salt concentration in moderately dilute solution.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a salt of weak acid and weak base:
\[ \text{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b) = \frac{1}{2} pK_w + \\frac{1}{2} pK_a - \frac{1}{2} pK_b \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the difference between \( pK_a \) and \( pK_b \):
\[ pK_a - pK_b = 4.76 - 4.75 = +0.01 \]
Divide by 2:
\[ \frac{1}{2}(0.01) = +0.005 \]
Compute the pH:
\[ \text{pH} = 7 + 0.005 = 7.005 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because acetic acid is infinitesimally weaker than ammonia (\( pK_a > pK_b \)), the solution is very slightly alkaline, giving a pH just above 7.00 at 7.005.
Final Answer: \( 7.005 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q14 - Molar solubility of barium sulphate from solubility product

questiontext.text:
The solubility product constant \( K_{sp} \) of barium sulphate (\( \mathrm{BaSO}_4 \)) in water is \( 1.1 \times 10^{-10} \) at 298 K. What is the molar solubility of \( \mathrm{BaSO}_4 \) in pure water?
(Given: \( \sqrt{1.1} \approx 1.05 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Solubility product: \( K_{sp} = 1.1 \times 10^{-10} \).
Square root value: \( \sqrt{1.1} = 1.05 \).
Medium: Pure water at 298 K.

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Barium sulphate dissolves as a 1:1 electrolyte: \( \mathrm{BaSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \). No common ions or competing complexation equilibria exist.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Let \( S \) be the molar solubility of \( \mathrm{BaSO}_4 \) in \( \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \).
At saturation: \( [\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}] = S \) and \( [\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}] = S \).
\[ K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}][\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}] = S^2 \]
\[ S = \sqrt{K_{sp}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \( K_{sp} \) into the expression:
\[ S = \sqrt{1.1 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{M}^2} \]
Separate the numerical coefficient and power of ten:
\[ S = \sqrt{1.1} \times \sqrt{10^{-10}} = 1.05 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Squaring \( 1.05 \times 10^{-5} \) yields \( 1.1025 \times 10^{-10} \), which reproduces \( K_{sp} \). The molar solubility is \( 1.05 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \).
Final Answer: \( 1.05 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q15 - Equilibrium concentration in water gas shift reaction

questiontext.text:
At 700 K, the equilibrium constant \( K_c \) for the water-gas shift reaction:
\[ \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \]
is 4.24. If 0.10 mol of \( \mathrm{CO} \) and 0.10 mol of \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \) are initially placed in a 1.0 L sealed reaction vessel and heated to 700 K, what is the equilibrium concentration of \( \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \)?
(Given: \( \sqrt{4.24} \approx 2.06 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Volume of reaction vessel: \( V = 1.0\ \text{L} \).
Initial amount of \( \mathrm{CO} \): \( n_{\mathrm{CO}} = 0.10\ \text{mol} \implies [\mathrm{CO}]_0 = 0.10\ \text{M} \).
Initial amount of \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \): \( n_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}} = 0.10\ \text{mol} \implies [\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}]_0 = 0.10\ \text{M} \).
Initial concentrations of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and \( \mathrm{H}_2 \): 0 M.
Equilibrium constant: \( K_c = 4.24 \) at \( T = 700\ \text{K} \).
Given square root: \( \sqrt{4.24} = 2.06 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Let \( x \) be the concentration (in \( \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1} \)) of \( \mathrm{CO} \) and \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \) reacted at equilibrium. At equilibrium:
\[ [\mathrm{CO}] = 0.10 - x \]
\[ [\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}] = 0.10 - x \]
\[ [\mathrm{CO}_2] = x \]
\[ [\mathrm{H}_2] = x \]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant expression is:
\[ K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{CO}_2][\mathrm{H}_2]}{[\mathrm{CO}][\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}]} = \frac{x^2}{(0.10 - x)^2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Take the square root of both sides of the expression:
\[ \sqrt{K_c} = \frac{x}{0.10 - x} \]
\[ 2.06 = \frac{x}{0.10 - x} \]
Multiply across:
\[ x = 2.06(0.10 - x) = 0.206 - 2.06x \]
Collect terms involving \( x \):
\[ x + 2.06x = 0.206 \]
\[ 3.06x = 0.206 \]
\[ x = \frac{0.206}{3.06} \approx 0.0673\ \text{M} \approx 0.067\ \text{M} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Substitute \( x = 0.0673\ \text{M} \) back to check:
\[ [\mathrm{CO}] = [\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}] = 0.10 - 0.0673 = 0.0327\ \text{M} \]
\[ \frac{(0.0673)^2}{(0.0327)^2} = \left(\frac{0.0673}{0.0327}\right)^2 = (2.058)^2 \approx 4.24 \]
The equilibrium concentration of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) is \( 0.067\ \text{M} \).
Final Answer: \( 0.067\ \text{M} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q16 - Equilibrium partial pressure in Boudouard reaction

questiontext.text:
Solid carbon reacts with carbon dioxide gas in a closed vessel at 1000 K according to the reaction:
\[ \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) \]
The equilibrium constant \( K_p \) at this temperature is 3.0 bar. If the total equilibrium pressure inside the vessel is 0.81 bar, what is the equilibrium partial pressure of \( \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) \)?
(Given: \( \sqrt{18.72} \approx 4.33 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total equilibrium pressure: \( p_{\text{total}} = 0.81\ \text{bar} \).
Equilibrium constant: \( K_p = 3.0\ \text{bar} \) at \( T = 1000\ \text{K} \).
Square root value: \( \sqrt{18.72} = 4.33 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The activity of pure solid carbon is unity. Total pressure is the sum of partial pressures of all gas species: \( p_{\text{total}} = p_{\mathrm{CO}} + p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} \). Therefore, \( p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 0.81 - p_{\mathrm{CO}} \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant \( K_p \) expression is:
\[ K_p = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO}}^2}{p_{\mathrm{CO}_2}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \( p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 0.81 - p_{\mathrm{CO}} \) into the \( K_p \) equation:
\[ \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO}}^2}{0.81 - p_{\mathrm{CO}}} = 3.0 \]
Expand and rearrange into standard quadratic form \( ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \):
\[ p_{\mathrm{CO}}^2 = 3.0(0.81 - p_{\mathrm{CO}}) = 2.43 - 3.0 p_{\mathrm{CO}} \]
\[ p_{\mathrm{CO}}^2 + 3.0 p_{\mathrm{CO}} - 2.43 = 0 \]
Apply the quadratic formula with \( a = 1 \), \( b = 3.0 \), and \( c = -2.43 \):
\[ p_{\mathrm{CO}} = \frac{-3.0 + \sqrt{(3.0)^2 - 4(1)(-2.43)}}{2(1)} \]
\[ p_{\mathrm{CO}} = \frac{-3.0 + \sqrt{9.0 + 9.72}}{2} = \frac{-3.0 + \sqrt{18.72}}{2} \]
Substitute \( \sqrt{18.72} = 4.33 \):
\[ p_{\mathrm{CO}} = \frac{-3.0 + 4.33}{2} = \frac{1.33}{2} = 0.665\ \text{bar} \approx 0.66\ \text{bar} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
If \( p_{\mathrm{CO}} = 0.66\ \text{bar} \), then \( p_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 0.81 - 0.66 = 0.15\ \text{bar} \).
Checking \( K_p \): \( \frac{(0.66)^2}{0.15} = \frac{0.4356}{0.15} = 2.904 \approx 3.0\ \text{bar} \). The partial pressure of \( \mathrm{CO} \) is 0.66 bar.
Final Answer: \( 0.66\ \text{bar} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q17 - Equilibrium constant for dinitrogen tetroxide dissociation

questiontext.text:
A sample of 13.8 g of \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4 \) is placed in a 1.0 L closed reaction vessel and heated to 400 K. At equilibrium, the total pressure is measured to be 9.15 bar according to:
\[ \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \]
What is the equilibrium constant \( K_p \) for this dissociation reaction at 400 K?
(Take molar mass of \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4 = 92\ \text{g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \) and \( R = 0.083\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4 \): \( m = 13.8\ \text{g} \).
Molar mass of \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4 \): \( M = 92\ \text{g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \).
Volume of vessel: \( V = 1.0\ \text{L} \).
Temperature: \( T = 400\ \text{K} \).
Total equilibrium pressure: \( p_{\text{total}} = 9.15\ \text{bar} \).
Gas constant: \( R = 0.083\ \text{L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The initial amount of \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4 \) produces an initial hypothetical pressure \( p_0 \) before dissociation. Dissociation degree \( \alpha \) increases total moles by a factor of \( (1 + \alpha) \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Initial moles: \( n_0 = \frac{m}{M} \).
Initial pressure: \( p_0 = \frac{n_0 R T}{V} \).
Total pressure at equilibrium: \( p_{\text{total}} = p_0(1 + \alpha) \).
Partial pressures: \( p_{\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4} = \frac{1 - \alpha}{1 + \alpha} p_{\text{total}} \), \( p_{\mathrm{NO}_2} = \frac{2\alpha}{1 + \alpha} p_{\text{total}} \).
Equilibrium constant: \( K_p = \frac{p_{\mathrm{NO}_2}^2}{p_{\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4}} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate initial moles and initial pressure:
\[ n_0 = \frac{13.8}{92} = 0.15\ \text{mol} \]
\[ p_0 = \frac{0.15 \times 0.083 \times 400}{1.0} = 4.98\ \text{bar} \]
Determine the degree of dissociation \( \alpha \):
\[ 9.15 = 4.98(1 + \alpha) \implies 1 + \alpha = \frac{9.15}{4.98} \approx 1.837 \implies \alpha = 0.837 \]
Calculate equilibrium partial pressures:
\[ p_{\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4} = \left(\frac{1 - 0.837}{1.837}\right) \times 9.15 = \frac{0.163}{1.837} \times 9.15 \approx 0.812\ \text{bar} \]
\[ p_{\mathrm{NO}_2} = \left(\frac{2 \times 0.837}{1.837}\right) \times 9.15 = \frac{1.674}{1.837} \times 9.15 \approx 8.338\ \text{bar} \]
Calculate \( K_p \):
\[ K_p = \frac{(8.338)^2}{0.812} = \frac{69.52}{0.812} \approx 85.6\ \text{bar} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Sum of partial pressures: \( 0.812 + 8.338 = 9.15\ \text{bar} \), exactly matching total pressure. The value of \( K_p \) is 85.6 bar.
Final Answer: \( 85.6\ \text{bar} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q18 - Calculation of pH for extremely dilute hydrochloric acid

questiontext.text:
What is the pH of a \( 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M} \) aqueous solution of hydrochloric acid (\( \mathrm{HCl} \)) at 298 K?
(Given: \( \sqrt{4.01} \approx 2.0025 \) and \( \log_{10}(1.051) \approx 0.0216 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration of strong acid \( \mathrm{HCl} \): \( c = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M} \).
Temperature: \( T = 298\ \text{K} \), where \( K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \).
Values provided: \( \sqrt{4.01} = 2.0025 \) and \( \log_{10}(1.051) = 0.0216 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Because the acid concentration is smaller than \( 10^{-6}\ \text{M} \), the autoionization of water cannot be neglected. Water contributes additional \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) ions alongside \( \mathrm{HCl} \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Let \( x \) be the concentration of \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) produced by water ionization:
\[ [\mathrm{H}^+]_{\text{total}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} + x \]
\[ [\mathrm{OH}^-] = x \]
\[ K_w = [\mathrm{H}^+]_{\text{total}}[\mathrm{OH}^-] = (1.0 \times 10^{-8} + x)x = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Formulate the quadratic equation:
\[ x^2 + (1.0 \times 10^{-8})x - 1.0 \times 10^{-14} = 0 \]
Solve for positive \( x \) using the quadratic formula:
\[ x = \frac{-1.0 \times 10^{-8} + \sqrt{(1.0 \times 10^{-8})^2 - 4(1)(-1.0 \times 10^{-14})}}{2} \]
\[ x = \frac{-1.0 \times 10^{-8} + \sqrt{10^{-16} + 4.0 \times 10^{-14}}}{2} = \frac{-1.0 \times 10^{-8} + \sqrt{4.01 \times 10^{-14}}}{2} \]
\[ x = \frac{-0.10 \times 10^{-7} + 2.0025 \times 10^{-7}}{2} = \frac{1.9025 \times 10^{-7}}{2} = 0.951 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{M} \]
Determine total hydrogen ion concentration:
\[ [\mathrm{H}^+]_{\text{total}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} + 0.951 \times 10^{-7} = (0.10 + 0.951) \times 10^{-7} = 1.051 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{M} \]
Calculate pH:
\[ \text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.051 \times 10^{-7}) = 7 - \log_{10}(1.051) = 7 - 0.0216 = 6.9784 \approx 6.98 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
An acidic solution cannot have a basic pH of 8.00. The contribution of water lowers the pH slightly below neutral 7.00 to 6.98, maintaining physical plausibility.
Final Answer: \( 6.98 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q19 - Degree of ionization of hydrofluoric acid solution

questiontext.text:
The ionization constant of hydrofluoric acid (\( \mathrm{HF} \)) at 298 K is \( 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \). What is the degree of ionization \( \alpha \) of \( \mathrm{HF} \) in a 0.02 M aqueous solution?
(Given: \( \sqrt{0.06426} \approx 0.2535 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Ionization constant of hydrofluoric acid: \( K_a = 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \).
Initial concentration: \( c = 0.02\ \text{M} \).
Square root provided: \( \sqrt{0.06426} = 0.2535 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Testing the Ostwald approximation gives \( \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{c}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-4}}{0.02}} = \sqrt{0.016} \approx 0.126 \) (12.6%). Because this exceeds 5%, the approximation \( 1 - \alpha \approx 1 \) fails, requiring the exact quadratic solution.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The exact equilibrium expression is:
\[ K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \]
Rearranging gives the quadratic equation:
\[ c \alpha^2 + K_a \alpha - K_a = 0 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \( c = 0.02 \) and \( K_a = 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \):
\[ 0.02 \alpha^2 + 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \alpha - 3.2 \times 10^{-4} = 0 \]
Divide the entire equation by 0.02:
\[ \alpha^2 + 0.016 \alpha - 0.016 = 0 \]
Apply the quadratic formula with \( a = 1 \), \( b = 0.016 \), \( c = -0.016 \):
\[ \alpha = \frac{-0.016 + \sqrt{(0.016)^2 - 4(1)(-0.016)}}{2} \]
Calculate discriminant:
\[ (0.016)^2 + 0.064 = 0.000256 + 0.064 = 0.064256 \]
Take the square root using the given value \( \sqrt{0.064256} \approx 0.2535 \):
\[ \alpha = \frac{-0.016 + 0.2535}{2} = \frac{0.2375}{2} = 0.11875 \approx 0.119 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Substituting \( \alpha = 0.119 \) back into \( \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \):
\[ \frac{0.02 \times (0.119)^2}{1 - 0.119} = \frac{0.02 \times 0.01416}{0.881} = \frac{0.0002832}{0.881} \approx 3.21 \times 10^{-4} \], matching \( K_a \). The degree of ionization is 0.119.
Final Answer: \( 0.119 \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q20 - Common ion effect on nickel hydroxide solubility

questiontext.text: The solubility product constant \( K_{sp} \) of nickel(II) hydroxide, \( \mathrm{Ni(OH)}_2 \), is \( 2.0 \times 10^{-15} \) at 298 K. What is the molar solubility of \( \mathrm{Ni(OH)}_2 \) in a 0.10 M aqueous solution of \( \mathrm{NaOH} \)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Solubility product of nickel(II) hydroxide: \( K_{sp} = 2.0 \times 10^{-15} \).
Concentration of sodium hydroxide: \( [\mathrm{NaOH}] = 0.10\ \text{M} \).
Temperature: \( T = 298\ \text{K} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Sodium hydroxide is a strong electrolyte that dissociates completely into \( \mathrm{Na}^+ \) and \( \mathrm{OH}^- \). The common ion effect suppresses the solubility \( S \) of \( \mathrm{Ni(OH)}_2 \), so the hydroxide contribution from dissolution \( 2S \) is negligible compared to 0.10 M.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Dissolution equilibrium:
\[ \mathrm{Ni(OH)}_2(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{OH}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \]
Solubility product expression:
\[ K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}][\mathrm{OH}^-]^2 \]
Total hydroxide concentration:
\[ [\mathrm{OH}^-] = 0.10 + 2S \approx 0.10\ \text{M} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Let \( S \) be the molar solubility, so \( [\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}] = S \).
Substitute into the \( K_{sp} \) expression:
\[ K_{sp} = S \times (0.10)^2 \]
Substitute the given \( K_{sp} \):
\[ 2.0 \times 10^{-15} = S \times (1.0 \times 10^{-2}) \]
Solve for \( S \):
\[ S = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-15}}{1.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{M} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the approximation: \( 2S = 4.0 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{M} \ll 0.10\ \text{M} \), proving the simplification is valid. The molar solubility in 0.10 M NaOH is \( 2.00 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{M} \).
Final Answer: \( 2.00 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{M} \)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of establishing liquid vapour equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Consider the following events that take place when a petri dish containing liquid water is introduced into a closed, dry chamber fitted with a mercury manometer at constant temperature:

  1. Water evaporates at a constant rate into the chamber headspace.
  2. The mercury level in the open limb of the manometer begins to rise as the pressure of water vapour increases.
  3. The rate of condensation increases as the concentration of water molecules in the vapour phase builds up.
  4. The rate of condensation becomes equal to the rate of evaporation.
  5. The mercury levels in the manometer become completely constant at a fixed height difference.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these events from the initial introduction of water to the final attainment of dynamic equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given System and Physical Context
A dish of pure liquid water is placed in a closed, dry box fitted with a mercury manometer at a fixed temperature \(T\). The system evolves towards dynamic liquid-vapour phase equilibrium: \[\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_2O(vap)}\]

Step 2: Sequence of Physical Events
1. Initially, no water vapour is present in the chamber. Water immediately begins to evaporate from the liquid surface at a constant rate that depends only on temperature and surface area (Event I).
2. As gaseous water molecules accumulate in the enclosed space, they exert pressure, causing the mercury level in the manometer's open limb to rise (Event II).
3. With the increasing concentration of water vapour molecules in the headspace, the frequency of molecular collisions with the liquid surface rises, progressively increasing the rate of condensation (Event III).
4. The rate of condensation continues to increase until it exactly matches the constant rate of evaporation (Event IV).
5. Once dynamic equilibrium is attained, there is no further net change in the number of vapour molecules, and the manometer levels become completely constant, recording the equilibrium vapour pressure (Event V).

Step 3: Check and Final Conclusion
The correct chronological order of the physical stages is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q02 - Chronological events in radioactive tracer equilibrium

questiontext.text:
In an experiment to demonstrate the dynamic nature of solid-liquid saturation equilibrium, radioactive sugar is utilized as described in the following steps:

  1. Excess non-radioactive sugar is dissolved in water at constant temperature until a saturated solution in contact with undissolved solid is established.
  2. A small amount of radioactive sugar crystals is added to this saturated solution.
  3. Radioactive sugar molecules dissolve into the solution phase while an equal number of non-radioactive sugar molecules deposit onto the solid crystals.
  4. Radioactivity is detected in both the solid sugar phase and the solution phase.
  5. The ratio of radioactive to non-radioactive sugar molecules in the solution phase reaches a constant, unchanging value.

What is the correct chronological sequence of these stages during the verification of dynamic equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Dynamic Saturation Equilibrium
In a saturated solution of a solute, dynamic equilibrium exists between the solid and dissolved states: \[\text{Sugar(solid)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sugar(solution)}\] At equilibrium, the rate of dissolution equals the rate of crystallization.

Step 2: Chronological Sequence of Experimental Events
1. First, a saturated solution of non-radioactive sugar is prepared at constant temperature so that the rate of dissolution equals the rate of crystallization (Event I).
2. Radioactive sugar crystals are then introduced into this saturated solution (Event II).
3. Because the equilibrium is dynamic rather than static, continuous exchange occurs across the phase boundary: radioactive sugar molecules pass into the liquid solution, while dissolved non-radioactive molecules crystallize out onto the solid phase at an equal rate (Event III).
4. Consequently, radioactive molecules become detectable in both the liquid solution and the solid crystalline phase (Event IV).
5. As the dynamic exchange continues, the distribution of isotopic molecules achieves statistical uniformity, and the ratio of radioactive to non-radioactive molecules in solution stabilizes at a constant value (Event V).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological order of the stages is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q03 - Decreasing sequence of polyprotic ionization constants

questiontext.text:
Phosphoric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_4}\)) is a tribasic acid that ionizes in aqueous solution in three consecutive steps:

  1. \(\mathrm{H_3PO_4(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2PO_4^-(aq)}\) with equilibrium constant \(K_{a_1}\)
  2. \(\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}(aq)}\) with equilibrium constant \(K_{a_2}\)
  3. \(\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}(aq)}\) with equilibrium constant \(K_{a_3}\)

Which of the following correctly arranges these three ionization stages in decreasing order of their ionization constants (\(K_a\)) and acidity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical Equations and Experimental Values
The three successive ionization equilibria of phosphoric acid at \(298\text{ K}\) are: \[\begin{aligned} \text{Step I: } & \mathrm{H_3PO_4(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2PO_4^-(aq)}, \quad K_{a_1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3} \\ \text{Step II: } & \mathrm{H_2PO_4^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}(aq)}, \quad K_{a_2} = 6.2 \times 10^{-8} \\ \text{Step III: } & \mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+(aq)} + \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}(aq)}, \quad K_{a_3} = 4.2 \times 10^{-12} \end{aligned}\]

Step 2: Physical Justification of the Ordering
In Step I, a positively charged proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) is removed from an electrically neutral \(\mathrm{H_3PO_4}\) molecule. In Step II, a proton must be removed from a negatively charged anion (\(\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}\)), which requires more energy due to electrostatic Coulombic attraction. In Step III, the proton is removed from a doubly negatively charged anion (\(\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}\)), which experiences an even stronger electrostatic pull.
Consequently, the tendency to lose a proton decreases sharply with each successive ionization step: \[K_{a_1} \gg K_{a_2} \gg K_{a_3}\]

Step 3: Check and Final Conclusion
Arranging the stages in decreasing order of their ionization constant gives: \[\text{Step I} > \text{Step II} > \text{Step III}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q04 - Stepwise procedure for weak acid equilibrium

questiontext.text:
To systematically calculate the degree of ionization (\(\alpha\)) and \(\text{pH}\) of an aqueous solution of a weak acid \(\mathrm{HX}\) using the standard chemical equilibrium approach, the following steps are performed:

  1. Identify all chemical species present before dissociation as Brønsted-Lowry acids or bases.
  2. Write balanced equations for all possible proton transfer reactions in the solution.
  3. Compare the equilibrium constants of the possible reactions to identify the principal reaction having the highest \(K_a\) and the subsidiary reactions.
  4. Tabulate the initial concentrations, changes in concentration in terms of \(\alpha\), and equilibrium concentrations for species in the principal reaction.
  5. Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the ionization constant expression of the principal reaction to solve for \(\alpha\), then calculate \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\) and \(\text{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\).

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of these analytical steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analytical Framework for Weak Electrolyte Ionization
The systematic calculation of equilibrium concentrations and \(\text{pH}\) for a weak electrolyte in water requires establishing the dominant chemical equilibrium before performing algebraic evaluations.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequence Formulation
1. Step I: Identify all starting species present in the mixture before dissociation (for example, \(\mathrm{HX}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)) and classify them as Brønsted-Lowry acids or bases.
2. Step II: Formulate balanced chemical equations for every conceivable proton-transfer reaction involving these species (for example, \(\mathrm{HX} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{X^-}\) and \(2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{OH^-}\)).
3. Step III: Compare the equilibrium constants (\(K_a\) versus \(K_w\)) to distinguish the principal reaction from subsidiary equilibria.
4. Step IV: Set up an equilibrium table (ICE table) listing initial concentrations, stoichiometric changes in terms of \(\alpha\), and equilibrium concentrations for the principal reaction.
5. Step V: Substitute the equilibrium algebraic expressions into the \(K_a\) expression, solve the resulting equation for \(\alpha\), determine the hydronium ion concentration \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\), and calculate \(\text{pH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The proper logical sequence is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q05 - Experimental sequence of nitrogen dioxide dimerization

questiontext.text:
The following steps are carried out in a laboratory demonstration investigating the effect of temperature on the chemical equilibrium: \[2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N_2O_4(g)} \quad (\Delta H^\circ = -57.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})\]

  1. Copper turnings are treated with concentrated nitric acid to generate reddish-brown \(\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\).
  2. The generated gas is collected in two identical sealed glass test tubes such that both exhibit the same intensity of brown colour.
  3. Both tubes are placed in a water bath at room temperature (\(298\text{ K}\)) for 8 to 10 minutes to reach equal reference equilibrium states.
  4. One tube is transferred into a freezing mixture at \(270\text{ K}\), while the other tube is transferred into hot water at \(363\text{ K}\).
  5. The tube in the freezing mixture becomes almost colourless, whereas the tube in hot water develops an intense, dark reddish-brown colour.

What is the correct chronological sequence of these experimental stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Description of the Experimental Procedure
The equilibrium investigated is: \[2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N_2O_4(g)} \quad (\Delta H^\circ < 0, \text{ exothermic})\] Here, \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is reddish-brown while \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) is colourless.

Step 2: Chronological Sequence of Experimental Events
1. Event I: \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) gas is initially prepared by the redox reaction of copper metal with concentrated nitric acid: \[\mathrm{Cu} + 4\mathrm{HNO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} + 2\mathrm{NO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\] 2. Event II: The gas is collected into two identical glass tubes and sealed to ensure identical initial amounts and optical path lengths.
3. Event III: Both sealed tubes are placed in a water bath at \(298\text{ K}\) for 8–10 minutes to establish an identical reference equilibrium composition.
4. Event IV: One tube is immersed in a freezing mixture (\(270\text{ K}\)) and the second tube is immersed in hot water (\(363\text{ K}\)).
5. Event V: According to Le Chatelier's principle, lowering the temperature shifts the exothermic reaction forward to form colourless \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\), while raising the temperature shifts the reaction in the endothermic reverse direction to form dark reddish-brown \(\mathrm{NO_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of the experiment is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q06 - Molecular and energetic sequence of dissolution

questiontext.text:
Consider the molecular-level stages and energetic transitions that occur during the dissolution of crystalline sodium chloride in water to form an aqueous solution:

  1. Solid \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) crystal consists of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions held in a rigid 3D lattice by strong Coulombic attractions.
  2. Water dipoles surround the surface ions, and the high dielectric constant of water (\(\varepsilon_r \approx 80\)) screens and reduces the electrostatic attractive force by a factor of approximately 80.
  3. Lattice enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H^\circ = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is absorbed to separate the ions from the crystal lattice into gaseous ions.
  4. Water dipoles orient their negative oxygen ends toward \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and positive hydrogen ends toward \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), releasing hydration enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H^\circ = -784\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
  5. Hydrated ions disperse freely in the liquid medium, accompanied by a favorable net entropy increase (\(\Delta S^\circ > 0\)) that drives the overall process to spontaneous dissolution.

What is the correct logical and chronological sequence of these molecular stages during dissolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initial Solid State and Electrostatic Conditions
In solid sodium chloride, oppositely charged ions are fixed in a face-centered cubic lattice governed by Coulomb's law (Stage I).

Step 2: Solvent-Solute Interaction and Screening
When placed into water, polar solvent molecules interact with surface ions. The high relative permittivity (dielectric constant \(\varepsilon_r \approx 80\)) of water drastically weakens the interionic electrostatic force: \[F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\] reducing the attractive force between \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) by a factor of 80 (Stage II).

Step 3: Lattice Dissociation and Hydration Energetics
Overcoming the lattice requires input of lattice energy (\(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H^\circ = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) (Stage III). As separated ions enter the solvent, ion-dipole hydration interactions release hydration enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H^\circ = -784\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) (Stage IV).

Step 4: Thermodynamic Dispersal and Spontaneity
Although the enthalpy of solution is slightly endothermic (\(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H^\circ = +788 - 784 = +4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), the transition from a rigid crystal to freely moving hydrated ions produces a large increase in entropy (\(\Delta_{\text{sol}}S^\circ > 0\)), making \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ < 0\) and driving spontaneous dissolution (Stage V).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of events is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q07 - Chronological response of perturbed hydrogen equilibrium

questiontext.text:
A closed rigid vessel contains an equilibrium mixture of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\), \(\mathrm{I_2(g)}\), and \(\mathrm{HI(g)}\) at \(731\text{ K}\): \[\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)} \quad (K_c = 49)\] At time \(t_1\), additional \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) is rapidly injected into the system at constant temperature. Consider the following sequence of events:

  1. The concentration of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) experiences a sudden instantaneous spike, while the concentrations of \(\mathrm{I_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HI}\) remain momentarily unchanged.
  2. The reaction quotient \(Q_c = \frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]}\) abruptly drops to a value significantly lower than \(K_c\).
  3. The rate of the forward reaction suddenly exceeds the rate of the reverse reaction (\(r_f > r_b\)).
  4. Concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) progressively decrease over time while the concentration of \(\mathrm{HI}\) steadily rises.
  5. The forward and reverse reaction rates become equal again (\(r_f = r_b\)), establishing a new equilibrium at time \(t_2\) where \(Q_c = K_c\).

Which of the following correctly describes the chronological order of these occurrences from the point of perturbation at \(t_1\) to the attainment of the new equilibrium at \(t_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Perturbation Analysis
Before time \(t_1\), the system is in dynamic equilibrium: \[Q_c = \frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]} = K_c = 49\] At time \(t_1\), adding \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas creates a sharp step-increase in \([\mathrm{H_2}]\), while \([\mathrm{I_2}]\) and \([\mathrm{HI}]\) are unchanged at that instant (Event I).

Step 2: Thermodynamic Driving Force and Kinetics
Because the denominator term \([\mathrm{H_2}]\) has increased, the reaction quotient immediately drops below the equilibrium constant, \(Q_c < K_c\) (Event II).
According to collision theory and the law of mass action, the increase in reactant concentration increases the collision frequency between \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\), causing the forward reaction rate to exceed the reverse reaction rate, \(r_f > r_b\) (Event III).

Step 3: Progression Toward New Equilibrium
As the net forward reaction proceeds, \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) are continuously consumed while \(\mathrm{HI}\) is continuously produced. Hence, \([\mathrm{H_2}]\) and \([\mathrm{I_2}]\) decrease gradually while \([\mathrm{HI}]\) increases (Event IV).
Finally, as product accumulates and reactants are consumed, the forward rate decreases and the reverse rate increases until \(r_f = r_b\). At time \(t_2\), a new dynamic equilibrium state is reached where \(Q_c = K_c\) (Event V).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of events is: \[\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV} \rightarrow \text{V}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q08 - Chronological order of selective sulfide precipitation

questiontext.text:
An aqueous solution contains \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), and \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ions, each at an initial concentration of \(0.01\text{ M}\).
